articles.title: Fuel, transport costs push inflation to 7.8% in October 2026
articles.summary: The PSA reported that headline inflation accelerated to 7.8% in October, marking the highest figure since February 2023, when it reached 8.6%.

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 11:31am

A gas station in Quezon City on Aug. 16, 2026 offers additional fuel discounts to partner public utility vehicle (PUV) drivers, on top of the recent increase of government fuel subsidy, to help lessen the burden of high fuel cost.
The Philippine STAR / Miguel de Guzman
MANILA, Philippines — Headline inflation accelerated to 7.8% in October, marking the highest figure since February 2023, when it reached 8.6%.

The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) reported on Thursday, November 5, that transport costs primarily drove the uptrend, with the index surging to 20.1% from 14.6% in September. Higher fuel prices also pushed up housing, water, electricity and gas indices to 9.3% from 8.4% in the previous month.
Food inflation, meanwhile, eased slightly to 6.4% from 6.8%, owing to slower annual increases in the indices of fish and vegetables.
Faster increases, however, were still seen in rice and corn prices, with inflation accelerating to 20.7% from 20.3% and 19.3% from 17.3%, respectively.
Core inflation also rose to 5.4%. An increase in the metric, which excludes volatile food and energy items, suggests broader price pressures affecting the country's economy.
The peso's purchasing power has been on a downward trend since January. Data from the statistics agency showed that a peso in September 2026 was worth only P0.68 relative to its 2018 base value.
As long as inflation remains above the central bank's 3% target, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) says the country will remain on a tightening cycle.
The central bank raised its key policy rate by 50 basis points to 5.5% in October, bringing total rate hikes to 125 basis points this year alone.
The BSP will next meet on December 17 and release its final monetary policy report on December 23.

articles.title: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case
articles.summary:
Wong, 30, has been imprisoned since 2020 and is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under national security law

Hong Kong activist

blocks.text: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong was sentenced on Thursday to 10 years in prison after pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”, his second conviction under a national security law that critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.

Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s 2014 pro-democracy demonstrations, submitted his plea in September. He had been accused of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
In his ruling, High ​court Judge William Tam ‌described Wong’s actions as “grave in nature”.

He said Wong had visited the US to seek foreign interference ahead of the national security law’s introduction in 2020, and continued to share posts on social media by Law calling for sanctions after it was enacted.
Wong’s role was to “supply his underground support” and “arouse the attention of foreign countries to bolster the cause” of exiled activists, the judge said.
He said Wong’s sentence will run concurrently with the remaining term of his previous national security offence.
Wong wore a dark blue shirt and thick rimmed glasses in court, and nodded and bowed as supporters waved.

The former student leader is already serving a prison term of four years and eight months, imposed in November 2024, for conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.

Wong, 30, gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests, which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared – with his trademark black-rimmed spectacles – on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.

When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.

The following year, Beijing introduced a sweeping national security law it said was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics say has been used to target political opposition, dissolve civil society groups and silence independent media.

articles.title: Mon Tulfo admits mistake in Romualdez report: 'I was fed the wrong report'
articles.summary: Columnist Ramon Tulfo apologized on Thursday for reporting that Leyte Representative and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez had snuck out of prison, saying he was given the wrong information.

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 11:17am
Columnist Ramon Tulfo apologized on Thursday for reporting that Leyte Representative and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez had snuck out of prison, saying he was given the wrong information.
In a Facebook post, Tulfo said it was “embarrassing and humiliating” to admit that he was fed the wrong information and accepted it as gospel truth.
He added worse was he passed it on to his readers who "trust me and took me on my word."
“I was fed the wrong report that former speaker Martin Romualdez could go in and out of jail,” he said.

“Complete with all the details like riding in an ambulance and the brownouts taking place so he would not be seen going out and coming back in,” he added. “No such thing happened when the facts started coming in yesterday.”
On Tuesday, Tulfo posted information from a source he referred to as his “tweety bird.”

He claimed that Quezon City Jail-Male Dormitory Superintendent Maria Lourdes Pacion allegedly switches off the facility's electricity whenever Romualdez leaves and returns, to prevent CCTV footage from being recorded.
This prompted the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology to launch an investigation into the claims.
The Sandiganbayan Third Division also ordered officials of the BJMP to testify on Thursday regarding the status of Romualdez in detention.
Tulfo said there’s no excuse for his blunder.
“I goofed. No excuses. I should have first checked and cross-checked that report I received on Romualdez,” he said. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Ex-law dean withdraws as defense witness in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: A former law school dean who was invited by the team of Vice President Sara Duterte has declined to testify for the defense.

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 10:59am
The Senate impeachment court votes on the threshold required to convict an impeachable official on Sept. 23, 2026, with 13 senator-judges voting in favor and one against.
Senate of the Philippines / Joseph Vidal via Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — A former law school dean who was invited by the team of Vice President Sara Duterte has declined to testify for the defense.

In a statement on Thursday, November 5, former University of St. La Salle College of Law dean Ralph Sarmiento said that he was declining the defense panel’s invitation to “preserve the independence” of his “constitutional law scholarship” and the impartiality of his legal views and opinions.
“I had not anticipated that these views might potentially become part of the impeachment proceedings,” Sarmiento said.
“After careful consideration, I have decided to decline participation as a witness in the proceedings,” he added.
Sarmiento said that he had already reached out to the defense team, asking it to withdraw its request for a subpoena or his appearance.
The former law school dean was supposed to be the first witness to be presented by the defense team.

In their manifestation, Duterte’s defense team said that Sarmiento was expected to provide testimony regarding legal and constitutional principles relevant to the case, with a specific focus on Article II of the Articles of Impeachment.

Article II accuses Duterte of culpable violation of the Constitution and betrayal of public trust over her alleged unexplained wealth, discrepancies in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs), and alleged failure to divest from business interests while serving as vice president.
Duterte’s defense team cited Sarmiento’s credentials as a professor of Political and Constitutional Law as evidence of his capacity as a witness.
The defense team’s spokesperson, Michael Poa, said that the panel respects his decision.
“We respect Dean Sarmiento’s personal decision and appreciate his initial consideration of our invitation,” Poa said.
“We wish him well in his continued contributions to constitutional discourse,” he added.
Other witnesses are also expected to be disclosed in subsequent filings for hearings scheduled for November 10, 11, 12, 13, 19, 20 and 23.

articles.title: BJMP: Romualdez has 'personal staff' while in detention; lawmaker never left jail
articles.summary: A personal staff of former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez is staying with the lawmaker in his cell in the New Quezon City jail, the jail warden of the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology…

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 10:58am

A personal staff of former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez is staying with the lawmaker in his cell in the New Quezon City jail, the jail warden of the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) on Thursday.

BJMP Jail Warden Lourdes Pacion made the testimony during the hearing on the status of Romualdez's detention amid allegations of columinist Ramon Tulfo that the former speaker is able to leave the BJMP facility as he pleases in an ambulance.
"He has personal staff to help him in his daily needs," Pacion said.
Asked by the anti-court if the personal staff of Romualdez stays with the lawmaker inside his cell, Pacion answered in the affirmative.
Mental state
Pacion said allowing a personal staff or an individual to look after a person deprived of liberty is allowed on a case-to-case basis.
"I allowed it because his mental state is not yet stable per my assessment. We cannot hire more personnel to attend to the personal needs of Congressman Romualdez," Pacion said.

"We are allowing personal staff to stay inside the jail for humanitarian consideration, or if the patient is not in good condition, because we cannot attend to all personal needs of the patient," Pacion added.
Tulfo on Thursday morning, meanwhile, clarified that his information of Romualdez leaving detention facility is "false."
“I was fed the wrong report that former speaker Martin Romualdez could go in and out of jail,” Tulfo said.
Ahead of Tulfo's clarification, Pacion told the anti-graft court that Romualdez never left the BJMP premises in ambulance or any other vehicle.

"We categorically deny that information, your honor. Since the commitment of Congressman Romualdez [in detention], he stays in his room (cell). Once in a while he goes in the sunny area [of the detention facility]. For court hearings, he goes to the court room [provided by the facility]," Pacion said
"He did not go out riding an ambulance or any other vehicle," Pacion added.
Given Tulfo's retraction, the defense team of Romualdez put on record that Tulfo's previous allegation was untruthful and detrimental to their client.
"That was very damaging to our client because it has the tendency to inflame the public," the Romualdez's defense team said. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: DOF endorses $20-M UAE grant for Pasig River rehab to OP
articles.summary: The Department of Finance (DOF) said Thursday it endorsed a proposed $20-million, or approximately P1.2 billion, grant from the government of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) to the Office of the…

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 10:50am

The Department of Finance (DOF) said Thursday it endorsed a proposed $20-million, or approximately P1.2 billion, grant from the government of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) to the Office of the President (OP) for the rehabilitation of the Pasig River.

In a statement, the DOF said the proposed grant will support the Pasig River Restoration Project (PRRP), which targets a 25% reduction in plastic and organic waste entering the Pasig River system over five years.
Unlike loans, grants are forms of development assistance that do not require repayment.

Moreover, the Finance Department said the proposed grant underscores the Philippines' continued efforts to mobilize international partnerships and development assistance for environmental rehabilitation initiatives.

“We thank the Government of the United Arab Emirates for extending its hand in partnership with us to rehabilitate one of our country's vital waterways. The proposed assistance would strengthen waste management efforts and help improve the quality of life of our people,” said Finance Secretary Frederick Go.

The DOF said the project would cover five key areas of intervention, namely waste recovery and interception; household waste segregation and collection; capacity-building and support for informal waste collectors; improved waste processing and recovery; and stronger enforcement against illegal dumping.
The Finance Department said it is seeking the necessary authority to negotiate the proposed agreement, including its terms and conditions.
Once authorized, the DOF said it will facilitate negotiations with the UAE government in coordination with concerned government agencies. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Alberta's governing UCP endorses proposed riding boundary changes as NDP reiterates concerns
articles.summary: Alberta's governing United Conservatives have officially endorsed changes to provincial riding boundaries that the Opposition NDP says it believes are “rigged” to help the UCP win the next election.

image.caption: A file photo of Alberta's provincial flag from July 2026. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New
Alberta's governing United Conservatives have officially endorsed changes to provincial riding boundaries that the Opposition NDP says it believes are “rigged” to help the UCP win the next election.
Justice minister defends rural-urban hybrid ridings, says such ridings already exist in Alberta
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 04, 2026 9:19 PM EST | Last Updated: 14 minutes ago
Premier Danielle Smith's UCP caucus, in a vote split along party lines, voted Wednesday to endorse the proposed riding changes and put the new boundaries into a bill to be debated in the house.
Justice Minister Mickey Amery has said he expects legislation to pass by the end of the year ahead of the scheduled election in October 2027.
The riding report came from a panel with a majority of members selected by the UCP.
The NDP alleges the report dilutes urban ridings in Lethbridge and Calgary by merging them with adjacent rural areas to favour the UCP in a process known as gerrymandering.

Gerrymandering, which is common in the United States, sees electoral districts drawn up not for reasons of shared geography and priorities but by voting patterns in order to assist one political party.

items: Province's last boundary panel chair urged new panellists not to alter southern Alberta ridings. They did.

blocks.text: Speaking during a debate of the proposals Wednesday, Amery defended the rural-urban hybrid ridings that have become the focus of debate, saying they already exist in Alberta.

"Hybrid ridings also do something else: they bring together communities that share services, employment, infrastructure and economic interests, regardless of whether a municipal boundary happens to run between them," said Amery.
With 2024 legislation, Smith's government removed the requirement that electoral boundaries respect municipal boundaries as a guiding principle.

The NDP has charged that the latest process to redraw the report was illegitimate from the start, and pleaded until the last minute for the UCP to instead revert to the map recommended by an independent public commission.
Nenshi said Wednesday that he believes the changes are designed to help vulnerable UCP ministers keep their seats.
"It strikes a knife into the heart of Alberta's democracy," he said.

items: New Alberta riding plan shifts thousands of Calgary, Lethbridge voters into rural-urban districts

blocks.text: The latest redrawing has been a controversial and complicated affair since the premier rejected the main recommendations of a public boundaries commission early this year. The commission came back with a split report.
Bucking political norms, Smith's government voted down the commission's majority position in the legislature and restarted the process with a new advisory panel.

Traditionally, Alberta's chief justice helps find a current or retired judge to chair and oversee the work. But earlier this year, the acting Alberta chief justice declined to participate, calling the new process "irregular."

The panel, chaired by retired Alberta justice Brian O'Ferrall, was given direction based on some recommendations from the previous commission's chair, including expanding the number of ridings to 91 from 87 to preserve two rural ridings that were to be dissolved.
Smith has said urban representation, amid population growth in cities, shouldn't come at the expense of rural Alberta.
But Nenshi told the house Wednesday the panel went well beyond those marching orders without justification and without considering public feedback.
Alberta panel proposes new electoral maps

The proposals would split the southern city of Lethbridge into four ridings from its current two. It would have one strictly urban riding while the other three would see some neighbourhoods linked to sprawling adjacent rural areas.
It also includes additional hybrid ridings for the west side of Calgary.
In question period earlier Wednesday, Smith called Nenshi's allegations "ridiculous," and said if anyone gerrymandered the maps to benefit the UCP, "they failed miserably."
She said under the proposed maps, if the UCP were to win the popular vote by the same margins as it did in the 2023 election, the NDP would gain three seats and the UCP would gain one.
"[Nenshi's] trying to set it up so that people will doubt the integrity of elections," she said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Lisa Johnson
The Canadian Press
Lisa Johnson is a reporter for The Canadian Press based in Alberta.
With files from Jack Farrell

articles.title: Pope Leo hosts Bob Dylan at official residence in Rome
articles.summary: Pope Leo had previously quoted Dylan's work in the preface of a book warning against nuclear rearmament.

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV hosted Bob Dylan at his official residence, the Apostolic Palace, on Wednesday during the Rome stop on the singer-songwriter's Italian tour.
Dylan, 85, wore a nearly all-black outfit, including a pulled up hoodie, gloves and umbrella, starkly contrasting with the Chicago-born Pope's all-white vestments.
The meeting between the pair, who both hail from the US Midwest, was brief, according to Vatican News.
Leo presented the Nobel laureate with a rosary and Dylan gifted Leo a copy of his autobiography, Chronicles: Volume One.
The visit happened ahead of Dylan's scheduled performance on Thursday at the Palazzo dello Sport, one of several Italian stops on his Rough and Rowdy Ways tour.
Leo has previously referenced Dylan in his own work, quoting Dylan's unreleased anti-nuclear song, Go Away You Bomb, in the preface to a book titled Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift.
"I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an' man-handled," was the line quoted in the book's warning to the world against rearmament.

The song was written in 1963 amid the Cold War, but was never recorded. The typewritten lyrics were unpublished until 2013 when they were discovered and put up for auction, according to the New York Times.
It was the second time Dylan had met a pope. In 1997 Dylan was invited to perform in front of Pope John Paul II and about 300,000 young people for the 23rd National Eucharistic Congress in Bologna.
Dylan played four songs including Knockin' on Heaven's Door, and reportedly climbed the stage mid-set to greet John Paul with a handshake and exchange a few words.
The then-Pope quoted Dylan's hit Blowin' in the Wind in his sermon to the crowd.

articles.title: Former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon enters witness box in Sydney double murder trial
articles.summary:
Lamarre-Condon gives evidence in court after pleading not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in early 2024

blocks.text: Former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon is giving evidence from the witness box in his double murder trial as his defence begins in Sydney.
Lamarre-Condon, 31, is accused of fatally shooting couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Lamarre-Condon on Thursday started giving evidence at the New South Wales supreme court in front of a 15-person jury. He was the first witness for the defence.
Wearing a light grey suit, a dark coloured tie and a white collared shirt, Lamarre-Condon vowed to tell the truth.

Prosecution lawyers wrapped up their case on Thursday morning. They called more than 50 witnesses, played hours of CCTV footage and shared pages of social media messages over the first seven weeks of the trial.
Lamarre-Condon’s defence team has previously claimed Baird and Davies were accidentally shot in two separate struggles with the accused when he was acting in “self-defence”.
The officer cleaned up the scene and disposed of the bodies afterwards because he “panicked considerably”, the defence lawyer John Stratton SC previously said.

articles.title: Former NASA chief economist named new head of Canadian Space Agency
articles.summary: Alexander MacDonald was named the new president of the Canadian Space Agency late Wednesday evening.

image.caption: The Canadian Space Agency’s David Florida Laboratory is seen in Ottawa on March 16. Alexander MacDonald was named the agency's new president on Wednesday. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Alexander MacDonald was named the new president of the Canadian Space Agency late Wednesday evening.
Alexander MacDonald helped establish the 'Moon to Mars' strategy that includes the Artemis mission
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly made the announcement in Ottawa during a tribute event to the late Marc Garneau, the first Canadian to travel to space.

MacDonald served as NASA's first chief economist, according to a government news release. In that role, he helped establish the "Moon to Mars" strategy, which includes the recent Artemis II mission that saw Canadian Jeremy Hansen travel around the moon earlier this year.
"As incredible as this year has been, I am even more excited about what the future holds for Canadians in space," MacDonald told the Ottawa crowd at Thursday's event.
"Space has never been more important for the strength and future of Canada, and never before has the world looked to Canada more for global leadership in the space domain."

items: Canada can't launch rockets on its own. A handful of companies want to change that

blocks.text: MacDonald takes over from Campbell

MacDonald is taking over from outgoing president Lisa Campbell, who had been in the role since 2020. His appointment comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney's government looks to expand Canada's space capabilities.
Earlier this month, Joly also appointed Hansen as a special advisor to the government on developing a new space strategy.

The federal government listed space-based platforms for surveillance as a key priority in its new defence industrial strategy released in February. The Carney government is also looking to expand co-operation with European countries in space as part of the proposed partnership with the European Union.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.

articles.title: PH holds nationwide earthquake drill for Q4 2026
articles.summary: The Philippines on Thursday conducted its Fourth Quarter Nationwide Simultaneous Earthquake Drill (NSED) featuring a magnitude 8.5 earthquake and tsunami scenario.

blocks.text: MAGNITUDE 8.5 QUAKE, TSUNAMI SCENARIO
Published November 5, 2026 9:34am
The Philippines on Thursday conducted its Fourth Quarter Nationwide Simultaneous Earthquake Drill (NSED) featuring a magnitude 8.5 earthquake and tsunami scenario.

The Office of Civil Defense (OCD) led the exercise in the designated main pilot area, Santa Ana, Cagayan, in collaboration with various government agencies, uniformed services, and local government units.

According to the OCD, the full-scale simulation featured an earthquake triggered by movement along the East Luzon Trough, with its hypothetical epicenter located 180 kilometers southeast of Santa Ana.
The exercise also included a tsunami scenario to test the government's preparedness and response capabilities in the event of a major earthquake.

The drill aimed to assess and strengthen the implementation of the government's Earthquake and Tsunami Contingency Plan, as well as the Regional Disaster Response Plan (RDRP) of the Cagayan Valley Regional Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (RDRRMC).—AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Filipino teens among least physically active globally — WHO study
articles.summary: Around 40% of Filipino adolescents reported no day with at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity in a week

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 9:26am
MANILA, Philippines — About two in five Filipino adolescents reported getting less than an hour of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, falling behind their counterparts around the world.
The World Health Organization's latest survey foudn tha taround 40% of adolescents aged 11 to 17 in the Philippines reported having no "active day" in a week.
An active day was defined as one with at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, such as brisk walking, cycling, playing sports or other activities that raise the heart rate.
The study, published in The Lancet Global Health, draws on hundreds of population-based surveys from 140 countries and territories, involving more than 3.2 million teens.

The Philippines was grouped with Namibia and Nepal, where around 40% of adolescents also reported no active days. By comparison, the global average was about 25%. This makes the Philippines' youth among the least active in the world.
Over the years, overall inactivity barely changed and even marginally declined in the Philippines, from 40.85% in 2010 to 40.32% in 2025.
Filipino girls are even less active than their male counterparts in the 2025 findings, with 42.7% reporting having no active day compared with 38% of boys.
The trend is similar globally. Only 11% of girls said they were active every day, compared with 17% of boys.
"For 15 years, the world has made almost no progress in getting young people moving, and girls are being left furthest behind," WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.
PHILIPPINES | WORLD HEALTH ORGANIZATION DATA
4 in 10 Filipino adolescents report zero active days
Percentage of adolescents reporting no physically active days in the previous week, 2021–2025
Source: World Health Organization, physical activity data, Philippines, 2021–2025.
Global progress stalls
Worldwide, one in four adolescents aged 11 to 17 reported no active days in the previous week, according to estimates published in The Lancet Global Health.
That amounts to around 240 million young people.
The study drew on 389 population-based surveys from 140 countries and territories involving more than 3.2 million adolescents.
On average, adolescents reported being active for 2.7 days a week, while only 14% said they were active for at least 60 minutes on all seven days.
The WHO warned that physical inactivity is a major risk factor for heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers.
"Helping young people develop active habits early in life is critical to protecting their health and reducing the global burden of these diseases," the agency said.
The study found little global progress over the past 15 years, with adolescent physical activity levels remaining virtually unchanged since 2010.
More than individual choice
The WHO said physical activity depends partly on the environments in which adolescents live, study and travel.

Access to safe public spaces, opportunities to walk or cycle, transportation systems, school environments, affordability and social norms can all affect how active young people are. Increasingly screen-centered lifestyles may also play a role.
"The answer is not to tell adolescents to try harder. It is to build schools, streets and communities where moving, playing and being active is safe, easy and normal," Tedros said.
The WHO called for stronger action across education, transport, urban planning, sports and health to make physical activity easier and safer for young people.
"Countries need policies that make physical activity an easy, safe and accessible part of everyday life," the agency said. — Camille Diola with Agence France Presse

articles.title: Beach weather in November? In Canada? These photos prove it
articles.summary: Parts of Ontario and Quebec have been experiencing record-setting temperatures this week, and people have been taking full advantage of it.

image.caption: A woman stands in the St. Lawrence River at Verdun Beach as temperatures soar in Montreal on Wednesday. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada·Photos
Parts of Ontario and Quebec have been experiencing record-setting temperatures this week, and people have been taking full advantage of it.
Parts of Ontario and Quebec have been basking in summer-like weather this week
Even at the best of times, it's hard to imagine swimming outdoors in November — no matter where you live in Canada. But 2026 is changing that conventional wisdom.
Parts of Quebec and Ontario have been experiencing potentially record-setting summer-like temperatures this week, with highs over 20 C.
Normal highs in major cities this time of year are around 10 C.
In Montreal on Wednesday, it was 22 C, but felt like 24 C. Good enough for a trip to the beach.
A woman enjoys the warm weather at Verdun Beach in Montreal on Wednesday. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

According to the Weather Network, the weather anomaly is due to a strong, high-pressure ridge off the U.S. East Coast and a warm front associated with a Colorado low — a low-pressure area caused by the Rocky Mountains that tends to track northeastward. Those systems combined are pushing warmer air into parts of Canada.
Toronto has also been warmer than normal.
With a high around 21 C in Toronto Wednesday, some people took to a hammock to enjoy the sunshine. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)
Wearing shorts in Toronto in November? Why not? This man took advantage of the warmth as he walked his dogs Tuesday. (Alex Lupul/CBC)
What’s behind the warm November weather in London?
El Niño effect
This year's strong El Niño is probably part of the story, too.
Bill Merryfield, a research scientist at Environment and Climate Change Canada, says El Niño usually affects Canada toward the end of the year, causing unusually mild fall and winter temperatures.

"This year's event is truly exceptional because this warming has already exceeded three degrees, which is well above that of any previous event and is expected to go even higher before the usual peak of El Niño in November or December," he said, referring to Pacific Ocean temperatures tied to the weather phenomenon.
Two people take a break on Parliament Hill during an unseasonably warm Nov. 4. (Dan Taekema/CBC)
It was a warm day under the fall foliage at Toronto's High Park. (Alex Lupul/CBC)
A cyclist in Toronto took advantage of the delayed start of cooler temps, too. (Alex Lupul/CBC)
People had the same idea in western Quebec, too.
With files from The Canadian Press

articles.title: Hubert Aiwanger, prominent German politician, found dead in Berlin hotel
articles.summary:
Police and prosecutors open investigation into death of the 55-year-old Bavarian state deputy leader

A prominent German politician was found dead in a Berlin hotel on Wednesday, police said,…

blocks.text: A prominent German politician was found dead in a Berlin hotel on Wednesday, police said, adding they had launched an investigation.
The cause of death of Hubert Aiwanger, 55, who was deputy leader of southern Bavaria state, was not immediately clear.
Police said in a statement he was “found dead in his hotel room” in the Berlin-Mitte district.
Police and prosecutors had opened a probe to “determine the specific cause and circumstances of death”, the statement said.

“The aim ⁠of the inquest is to establish the ​specific cause of death ‌and the ‌circumstances surrounding it, and to rule out any ‌possible third-party culpability,” police and prosecutors said in a statement. They gave no further details.

Aiwanger, head of the populist Free Voters party and also Bavarian economy minister, was in Berlin to attend the opening of an office for his party but missed the event as he was feeling unwell, the Bild daily reported.
His body was later discovered by police in the hotel, it said.
The Bavarian state premier, Markus Soeder, described Aiwanger’s death as an “absolute tragedy”.
“We are all deeply shocked. Our thoughts are now first and foremost with his family and his children,” he said.
Aiwanger’s party were junior partners in the regional Bavarian government led by Soeder’s Christian Social Union (CSU).

He had headed the Bavarian branch of the Free Voters since 2006. Under his leadership, the party made it into the state government for the first time in 2018, but never won enough seats to qualify for Germany’s federal parliament.
Aiwanger had faced national controversy in 2023 after reports emerged that he wrote an antisemitic pamphlet as a 17-year-old schoolboy, in which Auschwitz was described as an “entertainment quarter”.
He denied having written the pamphlet, though he has admitted to having had “one or a few copies” of it in his school bag. He apologised over the affair but refused to step down.
Aiwanger had two children and lived with his partner, German media reported.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: Russian hacker group claims to have posted B.C. school district information on dark web
articles.summary: CBC News has discovered a hacked database stolen from the Burnaby School District on a dark web site run by a prominent shadowy ransomware group believed to be operating out of Russia.
articles.byline: Jason Proctor, Jodie Martinson, Jon Hernandez, Ivan Angelovski

image.caption: Qilin, a group believed to be based out of Russia, provides tools for hackers to commit ransomware attacks in exchange for a cut of extortion profits. (Jonathan Hayward/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: A shadowy Russian ransomware group has posted screenshots on the dark web from what appears to be a database stolen from the Burnaby School District.

The group — which calls itself Qilin — claims to offer downloads of information allegedly taken during a massive data breach school officials have said included medical information, detailed learning assessments, and personal information about both staff and students.

items: Cybercriminals may have accessed medical diagnoses in Burnaby school district attack: officials

blocks.text: Qilin is renowned as a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) provider that offers tools and infrastructure to hackers anywhere in the world in exchange for a percentage of proceeds demanded from victims.

While CBC News has not downloaded the contents of the files themselves, the screenshot samples posted on the Qilin website contain school district letterhead and human resource categories attached to what appear to be bulky files of data.
'Harassment Investigations' and 'Discipline'

The September attack on the Burnaby School District raised alarms with parents and students who contacted CBC News concerned that children's data may be in the hands of cybercriminals bent on exploiting deeply personal information for profit.

Working with CBC's visual investigations team, CBC News located the database shortly after the school district warned parents in an email Tuesday that "the threat actor claims to have published files and information from this incident on the dark web."
Hackers breached computer systems belonging to the Burnaby School District in September. The information they stole has been posted to the dark web. (CBC News)
The files appear on Qilin's dark web site in what is effectively a multi-page listing of sets of data stolen from various agencies, companies and individuals worldwide.
According to the screenshots posted online, the files contain a terabyte worth of data and have allegedly been seen nearly 4,000 times since they were first posted publicly on Oct. 15.
Screenshots of the files include folders labelled "Harassment Investigations," "Discipline," "Payroll" and "Mental health and Wellness."
CBC News has not viewed the contents of the folders.
In a statement to CBC News, the Burnaby School District said it has shared "reliable information with staff and families as it becomes available."

"We have engaged an external expert to help confirm whether data from the Burnaby School District has in fact been posted on the dark web and, if so, the nature and extent of any affected information," the statement said.
Widespread concern
According to the school district, hackers gained access to the district's systems on Sept. 21. The perpetrators appear to have started posting information online almost immediately.

CBC News received numerous emails about the incident after district superintendent Karim Hachlaf wrote to families on Oct. 14 confirming that "files taken containing personal information were copied and stolen by the criminal parties responsible for the attack."

CBC's visual investigations team took this screenshot of the dark web site where data stolen from the Burnaby School District in September appears to have been posted. The site belongs to Qilin, a Russia-linked group that provides hackers with online tools in exchange for a cut of ransomware profits. (CBC News)

Hachlaf's note claimed "most of the information maintained by the district about students, parents and guardians remains secure" but noted that "some bus touring information, student intervention records and other student assessments" had been affected "in a limited and smaller number of cases."
The warning sparked widespread concern.
"Help, our school has compromised our children's identity," one parent wrote to CBC News in an email that contained a copy of Hachlaf's note.
"I am a current Grade 12 student in the Burnaby Schools District who's been affected," wrote one student.
"Currently students and families have received virtually no clear communication."
Crippling attacks on institutions

In recent years, Qilin has been tied to a series of crippling high-profile ransomware attacks — most notably a 2024 cyberattack on Britain's National Health Service that saw major London hospitals cancel operations and blood transfusions.
Just last month, Japanese authorities handed over a Russian national accused of being involved with Qilin in connection with a European ransomware attack to German authorities.
The files contain medical information, detailed learning assessments and personal information about both staff and students. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
Ransomware attacks on health-care services and school districts have risen around North America, with schools in the U.S and Canada being targeted.
More than 60 million students and nine million teachers in both countries were impacted by a data breach of educational software provider PowerSchool.

The Associated Press found files describing sexual assaults, private hospitalizations and parental abuse among troves of data dumped online by a ransomware group that demanded $1 million in exchange for 300,000 files stolen from a school district in Minneapolis.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security describes Qilin's business model as one in which "a core group of developers will sell or lease their ransomware variant to other threat actors, called affiliates; the core developers will support affiliates' deployment of their ransomware in exchange for upfront payment, subscription fees, a cut of profits, or all three."

According to a threat profile prepared by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services in 2024, Qilin has been operating since 2022, likely originating from Russia. The threat profile claims Qilin was observed "recruiting affiliates on a hacking forum" in 2023.

"Qilin is known to target organizations in various countries and industries, including education, healthcare and critical services, with geographical regions targeted including Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States, among others. The group's targeting appears to be opportunistic rather than targeted," the threat profile reads.

"Victims are directed to communicate with the attackers via dark web portals or encrypted messaging services, ensuring the attackers' anonymity and complicating law enforcement efforts to track interactions. Payments are demanded in cryptocurrencies … However, even after payment, there is no guarantee that victims will receive the decryption tools required to recover their data."
Seeking 'information they can use'

Chester Wisniewski, chief information security officer and director of Vancouver-based computer security firm Sophos, told CBC News that attacks on schools are particularly common at the start of the school year in September and October.

"They're vulnerable because they're serving a large portion of the public, and them being offline or unable to open the schools provides an enormous amount of public pressure to do something," Wisniewski said.

"Usually they're after payroll information, they're after medical and personal information they can use. They're trying to upset the staff and the parents of the students in the case of a school, to get them to apply pressure on the school to pay an extortion demand."

items: Central Okanagan students, staff targeted in cybersecurity breach

blocks.text: To that end, Wisniewski said the thieves "don't care about your kids' grades, but they might care about their disabilities, or their learning problems, or their behaviour problems, or sensitive information about the finances of the staff members that work in the school."
Wisniewski said the Burnaby School District is working with another firm to strengthen security. He added that the public should refrain from blaming the victim.
Despite the fears of parents, Wisniewski said past attacks on other school districts have rarely resulted in individual harm.

items: Cyberattack on Burnaby School District triggers widespread disruption, concerns about data leaks

blocks.text: "The odds of something happening to your child's information despite it being published on the dark web where criminals hang out — it's a pretty low risk," he said.
"But it's certainly something to be concerned about and take protective actions."

articles.title: 8 DPWH personnel suspended over Surigao del Norte projects
articles.summary: The cases involve allegedly incomplete but fully paid projects in Surigao del Norte.

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 8:05am
An undated photo of the Ombudsman office.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman has ordered the six-month preventive suspension of eight Department of Public Works and Highways personnel over alleged irregularities in fully paid but substantially incomplete projects in Surigao del Norte.
In a six-page order released Wednesday, November 4, the anti-graft body suspended seven engineers and one accountant while administrative cases against them are pending.
The Ombudsman said their continued presence in office could allow them to influence the proceedings.
"Sufficient grounds exist to impose preventive suspension on Respondents," the order said.

"Without delving into the merits of the case and based on the evidence submitted by Complainant, the allegations against Respondents appear to be supported by strong evidence at this stage," it added.
The preventive suspension is not a finding of guilt and may remain in effect for up to six months while the cases are being resolved.
The Ombudsman's Field Investigation Office II filed administrative complaints for conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service, grave misconduct and serious dishonesty.
The complaints allege that the DPWH paid in full for substantially incomplete projects under the Surigao del Norte 1st District Engineering Office, causing financial prejudice to the government.
According to the Ombudsman, evidence submitted by the Independent Commission for Infrastructure included a list of projects reported as completed despite incomplete deliveries.
The following personnel were placed under preventive suspension:

articles.title: P.E.I. health minister admits doctor recruitment has been 'underwhelming'
articles.summary: There was no ambiguity on the challenges faced in Prince Edward Island's health-care system from the health minister Wednesday.

blocks.text: PEI·New
There was no ambiguity on the challenges faced in Prince Edward Island's health-care system from the health minister Wednesday.
'The idea that everyone is going to have their own practitioner … is just not realistic,' he added
‘Our recruitment has been underwhelming’ admits P.E.I. health minister of physician hiring
There was no ambiguity on the challenges faced in Prince Edward Island's health-care system from the health minister Wednesday in the legislature.

Responding to Liberal MLA Gord McNeilly asking about Islanders waiting for access to primary care, Health Minister Cory Deagle said things need to be done differently, adding "we can't just use the excuse that it's bad everywhere" and called recruitment "underwhelming."

"The idea that everyone is going to have their own practitioner … is just not realistic," Deagle said. "We have to affiliate to the entity," he added, meaning Islanders could be cared for by those on a team in a patient medical home.
"I think Health P.E.I. has made significant strides over the last eight months to do that … and we're going to see good progress coming in the months ahead."
Then-P.E.I. premier Dennis King in 2023 promised to eliminate the patient registry by April 2025. (Julien Lecacheur/Radio-Canada)

In 2023, then-premier Dennis King promised to eliminate the patient registry by April 2025 by having every Islander signed up for care with a doctor or nurse practitioner. However, more than 30,000 Islanders are still waiting.
An email from the province to CBC News states that so far in 2026, 24 additional physicians have been recruited, 18 of whom are specialists and six family doctors.
'One of the worst' for hip, knee waits

Answering questions Wednesday from Progressive Conservative Summerside-Wilmot MLA Tyler DesRoches about hip and knee replacement wait times, Deagle told question period "it's not good," and said the province is "actually one of the worst within Canada."
According to the province's numbers, a wait can be more than two years.

items: UPEI patient medical home down to 2 nurse practitioners from 5
'Attached to a team': One patient medical home will take a new approach to Islanders' health care

blocks.text: "I do think that we can get to a place where everyone either has a family physician or is affiliated to a patient medical home, which is the model we want to move towards, which is the UPEI patient medical home," Deagle told CBC News outside of question period.

"I think we can make good progress in that. I think we're doing that at UPEI. This is not something that's being experimented on. It's done in provinces across Canada ... and it's how we're going to recruit physicians [and] nurse practitioners to P.E.I."
Deagle said the number of people on the patient registry has decreased by about 5,000 and some doctors have been recruited.
Default Caption: P.E.I. Health and Wellness Minister Cory Deagle was blunt about the challenges the province's health-care system is facing when questioned Wednesday. (P.E.I. Legislative Assembly)

He is confident patients can be connected with medical homes and said the UPEI patient medical home is not necessarily a new concept, though it is to the province, and changing a system doesn't necessarily come easily.

"What we've done over the summer is work with the medical society, the nurses' union, all the folks that are involved, to sit down with them and go over, how is this model going to work to affiliate to the building itself, to the patient medical home, not necessarily the prescriber," he said.

"I think those consultations have been excellent. For once, they actually feel like we're sitting down with them before we implement something to hear their feedback. And I think because of that and the trust that we've built up with these organizations, these groups, I think this can be successful at UPEI."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Lucas McInnis is a journalist at CBC Prince Edward Island. He can be reached at lucas.mcinnis@cbc.ca.
With files from Wayne Thibodeau

articles.title: Milburn review to call for jobs ’revolution’ for young people with disabilities
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Government should introduce ‘flexi-jobs’ alongside subsidies and skills support, former minister will say

The British state should create and subsidise paid jobs…

blocks.text: The British state should create and subsidise paid jobs for thousands of disabled young people as part of an “opportunity revolution” aimed at reversing years of labour market discrimination, the Milburn review of youth employment will recommend.

The review, due to report this month, will say the government should introduce “flexi-jobs” alongside employment subsidies and intensive skills support to make it easier for disabled and chronically ill 16- to 24-year-olds to get work.

It will argue that the state should step in to underwrite jobs for young people who are locked out of employment and training opportunities, as part of an overhaul of what it sees as an outdated welfare and skills system.

About a million young people are now classified as “Neet”, meaning they are not in education, employment or training. Nearly half (45%) of those are disabled or in ill health. Disabled young people are three times as likely to be Neet as their non-disabled peers.

The review’s author, the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, has described soaring numbers of Neets as a moral and economic crisis, warning that failure to tackle rising youth disengagement from work risks creating a “lost generation”.

He has rejected what he has called “myths” about young people being “snowflakes”, insisting that the crisis in youth mental health is real, most youngsters want to work, and it is the duty of government and employers to provide support and opportunities.

The review will say young people with disabilities need a flexible and supportive approach to work that acknowledges fluctuating medical conditions and lack of work experience, and recognises the importance of part-time roles in helping them build confidence.

One eye-catching recommendation is for the UK to adopt a Danish-style “flexi-job” scheme. This guarantees disabled participants employment while allowing them to set working hours – in some cases starting with as few as four hours a week – that suit their individual capacities, with wages topped up by the government.

It will also call for creative ways of shaping jobs to individual capabilities, such as “job carving”: splitting the three component parts of a single entry-level role and matching youngsters to each of those roles. A retail role that comprises stock-filling, till work and locking up would become three job opportunities.

Nearly half of 24-year-old Neets have never worked, and Milburn argued in his interim report earlier this year that abandoning a cohort of Covid-era youngsters coping with high levels of depression, anxiety, autism and ADHD would have a scarring effect on their life chances and lifetime earnings.

Although the government has said it will not endorse “crude cuts” to benefits, Milburn has suggested that the state should switch some of the £4bn a year it spends on disability benefits for young people into comprehensive, high-quality employment and training support.

However, he will probably face pushback from campaigners, and potentially backbench Labour MPs, who argue that job support should not be funded by disability benefit cuts that would push many young people into poverty and further away from the job market.

Milburn’s proposals are in part a recognition that young people with disabilities face huge barriers around recruitment processes and inflexible job design, and many businesses are unlikely to create job opportunities for them without government support.

The plans have echoes of the postwar Remploy scheme, which created state-funded workplaces providing “sheltered” employment for disabled ex-service personnel. At its height, Remploy had 90 factories across the UK, the last closing in 2013.
The review will urge large employers to voluntarily adopt employment targets for disabled 16- to 24-year-olds, although it is expected to stop short of recommending statutory quotas.

As well as creating jobs, the review will call for a boost for job support, including supported internships, placements, specialist job matching and coaching, and support for employers to provide workplace adjustments.

Milburn who has been critical of the limited ambitions of existing government job support programmes, has previously called for a “turbo-charging” of specialist internships for young people with special educational needs who are moving on from school and college.

The most common conditions reported by disabled Neets were depression, bad nerves or anxiety (23.8%), followed by autism (22.7%) and other health problems or disabilities (18.5%), according to the latest official figures.

articles.title: Law professor Dean Ralph Sarmiento declines to testify in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: Law professor Dean Ralph Sarmiento has declined to testify as a witness for Vice President Sara Duterte's defense team in her impeachment trial.

blocks.text: Filtered By: Topstories
News
Published November 5, 2026 7:52am
Law professor Dean Ralph Sarmiento has declined to testify as a witness for Vice President Sara Duterte's defense team in her impeachment trial.
In a video posted on Facebook, Sarmiento cited as reason the need to preserve his independence and impartiality as a constitutional law expert.

"I have decided to decline participation as a witness in the proceedings. This is a personal decision to preserve the independence of my constitutional law scholarship and the impartiality of my legal views and opinions," Sarmiento said in his post.
Sarmiento said he already communicated with Duterte's defense team to request the withdrawal of its subpoena request for his appearance before the Senate impeachment court.
If a subpoena has already been issued, he asked the defense team to seek its recall.
Sarmiento still thanked the defense team for recognizing the value of the constitutional and legal views he had shared on social media.
However, he pointed out that he had not anticipated that his opinions could potentially become part of the impeachment proceedings.
Duterte's defense team listed Sarmiento as its first witness in the unexplained wealth charges against the vice president.
On Wednesday, the defense team filed a request for a subpoena before the Senate impeachment court, with Sarmiento expected to take the witness stand on November 9.
Sarmiento is a professor of Political and Constitutional Law at the University of St. La Salle College of Law. He also previously served as the university's vice chancellor for administration.
He had earlier called for fairness in Duterte's impeachment trial following the prosecution's decision to drop three of the four charges against the vice president. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
articles.summary: Authorities in British Columbia say evidence suggests an animal may have been involved in the women's deaths.

blocks.text: A mother and daughter have died after a suspected grizzly bear attack in the Canadian province of British Columbia, their family has announced.

The women - identified as Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20 -were reported missing on 1 November when they did not return from what was supposed to be a short afternoon walk, the family said.
Their remains were found in a trail area in Bella Coola, according to the BC Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS), which said evidence at the scene "suggested an animal may have been involved".
Conservation officers are working to track down any bears involved.
Balcarras' remains were found on Monday and Reed's on Tuesday during search efforts by conservation officers and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).
Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the BCCOS, said it was not yet clear if more than one was potentially involved in the women's deaths.

He added that any captured bear would be assessed and if it is found to have been involved in the attack "it will be dispatched in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh Balcarras, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Balcarras had recently moved to Bella Coola to pursue a new career and begin a new chapter in her life, according to an online fundraiser to help the family with funeral costs.
Grizzly bears are listed as a species of "special concern" under federal legislation, and are an important part of the British Columbia landscape, according to Environmental Reporting BC, external.
Between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears are estimated to live in the province, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks, which has classified them as vulnerable.
According to the ministry, conflicts between bears and humans are "relatively rare" unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs and food.
But there have been a number of attacks in British Columbia in recent years.
A grizzly bear injured two hikers in the McGregor Mountain area in October 2025, one of whom died later due to critical injuries. The bear was later found dead.
The following month, a bear attacked a school group - also in the Bella Coola area - injuring 11 people.
The BC Wildlife Federation (BCWF) has said that reports of grizzly-human conflicts have risen since the province introduced a ban on hunting grizzly bears for sport in 2017.
"With no hunting pressure, grizzlies and humans will increasingly occupy the same spaces with inevitable consequences," the BCWF's executive director Jesse Zeman said at the time.

articles.title: Unmanaged menopause symptoms cost Canada's economy $3.5B, experts tell MPs
articles.summary: Unmanaged menopause symptoms are not just impacting women, but costing the Canadian economy $3.5 billion and 540,000 lost workdays every year, according to the Menopause Foundation of Canada.

image.caption: Trish Barbato, left, and Janet Ko are co-founders of the Menopause Foundation of Canada. (Brenda Witmer/CBC)

blocks.text: Politics
Unmanaged menopause symptoms are not just impacting women, but costing the Canadian economy $3.5 billion and 540,000 lost workdays every year, according to the Menopause Foundation of Canada.
Health transition affects 25% of Canada's workforce, according to the Menopause Foundation of Canada
"Menopause is more than a health issue. It is a workforce issue, an economic issue and a public policy issue," said the foundation's co-founder and president Janet Ko.
"But women lose, too — $3.3 billion in income through reduced hours, lesser roles or leaving work altogether."

Ko and the foundation's other co-founder and director Trish Barbato spoke to the House of Commons committee on the status of women on Wednesday advocating for measures to improve working conditions and health care for women and people experiencing menopause.
"When the symptoms of menopause go unaddressed, they become a barrier to women reaching their full potential, and Canada pays the price," Ko said.
The first and most important priority, according to Barbato, is to train providers and make menopause education mandatory in medical training.

items: Years-long wait to see a gynecologist has N.S. woman considering care elsewhere

blocks.text: "This is the greatest barrier today for women. They cannot get the help they need," Barbato said. "Federally, we are asking for a national quality standard on menopause care."
Another high priority is supporting workers, according to the foundation.

"Employers are far ahead of other areas in our agenda because they have realized that supporting women during this period is not only the right thing to do, but it supports their bottom line," Barbato said.
According to Barbato, over 250 Canadian employers have signed on to the foundation's campaign "Menopause Works Here" including Sunlife, BMO, PWC, Ikea, Metrolinx and Horizon Health.
"Five million working women in Canada are over 40 … they are skilled, they are capable, they are experienced and a high-value cohort that employers cannot afford to lose," Barbato said.
"Yet more than half a million workdays are lost each year due to unmanaged symptoms."
Calls for workplace action plans

Barbato also suggested a review of benefit programs and ensuring coverage of hormonal and non-hormonal benefits for menopause, using the Bank of Montreal as an example — which has added enhancements including pelvic floor therapy.

The foundation also recommends that Canada follow in the United Kingdom's footsteps and make menopause inclusive workplace action plans mandatory for large employers. From early 2027, U.K. employers with over 250 employees will be required to publish a menopause action plan under the country's 2025 Employment Rights Act.

"Women over 40 make up one-quarter of Canada's population, and one-quarter of its workforce, the largest share in the nation's history," Ko said. "They are in their peak working years, but too many are reaching this stage without the information, care and support they need to thrive."
Committee MPs recounted their own experiences with menopause and perimenopause after the founders' testimonies.

"You're entering menopause at the same time you're really becoming at the top of your career, and that could be attributed to burnout in a lot of cases," said Conservative MP Kelly DeRidder. "I'm actually starting to question myself: am I burnt out or am I going through menopause? I don't know."
Conservative MP Anna Roberts said she had lost count of the number of years she's gone through menopause.

Liberal MP Marie-Gabrielle Ménard referenced the research of Dr. Kevin Whittingstall, director of the Université de Sherbrooke's medical imaging and radiation sciences department, which was presented to the committee at an earlier meeting in late October.
Whittingstall told the committee menopause increases the risk of strokes, cognitive decline and dementia.

items: 'We can’t deal with it in Canada': Some women turn to Mexico for endometriosis care

blocks.text: "Yet despite affecting virtually every woman, menopause has received only a fraction of the scientific attention devoted to other major health conditions," Whittingstall said, citing how diabetes research in Canada has received roughly $300 million in the past 10 years, while menopause research has only received $20 million.
Whittingstall said he believes Canada has "all the expertise" to become a leader in the field.

"Certain countries have put a lot of effort into promoting brain research across menopause," Whittingstall said. "The interest is there. It's Canada's turn to show we can do just as well, if not better."
According to Barbato, the numbers tell a story that has been a "part of the taboo and stigma" that comes with talking about menopause.
"Women have just had to deal with this on their own, they felt very alone and they certainly were not bringing it up at work," Barbato said. "That stigma and difficulty still exists today.
"The burden is on the woman. In her income, in her ability to have a Canada pension later in life, her retirement income, there is so much weight of that cost."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sophia Laporte is an intern with CBC's Parliamentary Bureau in Ottawa and a fourth-year journalism and humanities student at Carleton University.

articles.title: Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'
articles.summary: Even for countries where typhoons are a way of life, the last few months have brought unusually wild weather.
articles.byline: Joel Guinto, Kurumi Mori, Darren Bett

blocks.text: Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'
Image source, Getty Images
Fishermen return to sea under a crimson sky in August after China's Jiangsu province is hit by Super Typhoon Dolphin
ByJoel GuintoBBC NewsReporting fromSingaporeKurumi MoriTokyo correspondent and Darren BettLead weather presenter
Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.

A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.

In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.

Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts: hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.
Typhoon Champi hit Taiwan and Japan
Source: NASA
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.

It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El Niño, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.

In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.

blocks.caption: Image caption, This riverside park in the south-eastern Chinese city of Nanning was submerged by Tropical Storm Narra

blocks.text: Image source, VCG via Getty Images
This riverside park in the south-eastern Chinese city of Nanning was submerged by Tropical Storm Narra
August brought Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days - before slamming into eastern China, triggering heavy floods and dozens of casualties.
Later that month Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three south-eastern Chinese cities over one week, shutting transport networks and forcing thousands to evacuate.

blocks.caption: Graphic showing the track of Typhoon Dolphin towards eastern China in August 2026.

blocks.text: 'Burning with fever'

The Pacific Ocean, heated to record levels by El Niño, is now brimming with typhoon energy, according to the Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) metric which measures the total intensity of a season's storms. This year, the ACE reading for South East and East Asia is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average.
El Niño also affects wind patterns and in this case, that means typhoons are tending to form further east than usual. They are also becoming stronger as they remain over warm waters for longer.

blocks.caption: Graphic showing the track of Typhoon Champi towards Taiwan and Japan in October 2026.

blocks.text: The Pacific can be likened to someone "burning with fever", says Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau. "It can go into convulsions soon," she said at a press briefing in Manila in September.

Forecasts suggest the worst may not be over. Last month, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific - the area monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency for its El Niño predictions - soared to 4C above normal, the highest since records began in 1949. The previous record - 3.6C - was set in December 1997.
China's climate agency has warned of sea surface temperatures continuing to rise over the next three months because of the El Niño.
Despite typhoon season usually peaking around September to October, this is likely to raise concerns across a region that has already been battered by back-to-back storms.

blocks.caption: Image caption, China has seen back-to-back typhoons as the 2026 El Niño intensifies

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
China has seen back-to-back typhoons as the 2026 El Niño intensifies
'Very, very scary' simulations

In August, Typhoon Chan-Hom baffled storm watchers in Japan by crossing the country from east to west, as opposed to the usual south-to-north trajectory. Japan's well-resourced and prepared authorities were able to evacuate people swiftly, but this would be far more challenging in some neighbouring countries.

To get a better picture of how rising temperatures could amplify the risks, Manila-based climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and colleagues simulated the effects of warmer conditions on the Philippines' most recent monster storms, including 2013's Super Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) which killed more than 6,000 people.

They arrived at what she describes as "very, very scary findings": higher temperatures increased total accumulated rainfall by 26%. It's a devastating prospect in a country where flooding from monsoon rains and some 20 tropical storms per year has emerged as one of the main disaster risks.

In recent years, floods have paralysed entire cities for days, and tired of the annual ordeal, Filipinos have taken to the streets to protest against corruption which they say is gnawing away at millions of dollars from flood-control projects.
Delfino, in an article on the University of the Philippines website, insists leaders and officials must gain a better understanding of climate hazards if communities are to be better prepared.
Tide of rubbish blankets Philippines river in August after weeks of monsoon rains
Preparing for the onslaught

Countries are bracing for the immediate impact. Japan has urged citizens to stockpile food and essentials for the typhoon season, and to secure outdoor furniture that could become deadly projectiles when typhoon winds hit. China has asked local officials to identify vulnerable areas and is upgrading its warning and monitoring systems.
The Philippines and its South East Asian neighbours are preparing for disruptions to food production, especially rice, and have increased support for famers, including the provision of fertilisers.
But what happens in the long term is less clear. The window for governments to act on El Niño is "closing", the United Nations Development Programme in Asia and the Pacific said recently.

"How severely a community experiences an El Niño is decided years in advance, by where roads and settlements are built, how water is managed, who is covered by social protection and whether public budgets have room to absorb a shock.
"Every El Niño tests the resilience we have built; this one should also drive us to build more," it added.

articles.title: Democrats take House and Senate from Republicans in US midterm rout
articles.summary: Democrats will control both chambers of Congress after flipping seats in Republican strongholds across the US in an election seen as a repudiation of President Donald Trump.

image.caption: Texas is sending a Democrat to the US Senate for the first time since 1988Image: Mike Segar/REUTERS

blocks.text: By late Tuesday night, it was clear that Democrats had succeeded in turning the 2026 US midterm elections into the so-called "blue wave" that had been predicted by pollsters.
But by Wednesday morning, the scale of the victory had turned into a "blue tsunami," surprising even the most optimistic political pundits.
In January, Democrats are set to have a commanding majority of at least 237 to 139 in the House and a 54 to 44 advantage in the Senate.
Democratic candidates flipped seven highly competitive Senate seats, including in what have for decades been reliably Republican districts in "red" states.
Texas voted in James Talarico as its first Democratic Senator since 1988, while electing a Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, for the first time in over 30 years.
The heartland state of Kansas, where farmers have been hit by high diesel prices and tariffs, will send a Democrat, Adam Hamilton, to the US Senate for the first time in over 90 years.
Other surprise wins in Republican strongholds included Iowa, South Carolina, and Ohio.
Big Democrat victory in US midterm elections

According to data analyzed by the New York Times, the 2026 Democrats came in at a 13 point margin of victory over the Republicans for the popular vote in the House, the largest such margin since 1976 seen in the wake of the Watergate scandal that shattered the presidency of Republican Richard Nixon two years prior.

Democrats also saw large gains in almost every voter group compared with the 2024 presidential election that put Trump in the White House, indicating the breadth of the political swing away from Republicans.
The full scale of the Democrat majority in both chambers may not be known until later Wednesday or Thursday as some races are still too close to call, or take longer to count ballots.
Democrats promise change, buoyed by Trump's unpopularity
The midterms were seen as a referendum on President Donald Trump, who had historically low approval ratings of around 38% ahead of election day.
Trump had campaigned relentlessly in the weeks leading up to the election, in what often turned into meandering speeches to dwindling crowds.

Democrats were able to capitalize on Trump's unpopular policies like the war in Iran and ensuing record-high fuel costs, which compounded a growing affordability crisis while the president was seen as enriching himself.
On Wednesday, Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries said his party was focusing "relentlessly on affordability and on accountability."

"The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over," said Jeffries, who could become the first Black speaker of the House in January.
Democrats say they are ready to launch a 100-day agenda to lower costs for fuel, groceries and healthcare, while conducting vast oversight and investigations into Trump and his administration.
When asked about the option of impeaching Trump or cabinet members for breaking laws while in office, Jeffries said Democrats were not focusing on that for now.
The margin of victory in the Senate is still not a two-thirds supermajority, with which Democrats alone could vote to convict in cases of impeachment, or override presidential vetoes.
Even as a lame duck president for the remaining two years of his term, Trump still has the power of the executive at his disposal, which comes with broad sway, especially in foreign policy.
Midterms put US political divide on display
GOP blame game begins

Despite for months claiming that Democrats would cheat to win the election, Trump did not dispute the Republican blowout. Instead, he claimed that Republicans would have won had his name been on the ballot.
Nevertheless, Trump said he would be willing to work with Democrats, while at the same time promised to use veto power to block legislation.
In remarks on Wednesday outside of his ballroom construction site at the White House, Trump appeared to admit that the economic impacts of the Iran war had cost the Republican Party.

blocks.caption: Trump preferred to speak more about ballroom project than the midterms on WednesdayImage: Evan Vucci/REUTERS

blocks.text: "I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term," Trump said.
Earlier Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance was more direct, saying the Iran war was the "reason we lost."
However, Trump spent the majority of the time in front of reporters on Wednesday talking about his ballroom project.
"It's going to be not only one of the biggest, but it'll be the most beautiful ballroom I think anywhere in the world," he said.
Republican supporters react: People are voting out of 'anger'

Future of department store in jeopardy after administrators appointed on Thursday morning

blocks.text: Australia’s premier upmarket department store David Jones has collapsed into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk and leaving the future of the 188-year-old retailer hanging in the balance.

The upheaval follows years of steep losses and underperforming stores that left the heritage retailer falling behind on rent, culminating in a breakdown of negotiations with its primary landlord, Westfield owner Scentre Group.

Staff were informed on Thursday that the David Jones board had appointed voluntary administrators from McGrathNicol, before the retailer’s main financier promptly installed FTI Consulting as receivers.
Under the dual appointment, FTI will take day-to-day control of operations, running the department store network while it restructures the business.
The process will almost certainly trigger immediate store closures, though receivers will try keep the core network open while hunting for fresh capital.
David Jones employs more than 6,000 staff across a network of 38 stores.
