articles.title: An Afghan teen won a full scholarship to a B.C. school. But Canada denied her study permit
articles.summary: Immigrant advocates say Canada regularly rejects study permits from Afghan women and girls, even when they have full scholarships, despite the fact that they face some of the strictest barriers to…

image.caption: Afghan primary school girls attend class at a school in Kandahar on Sept. 7, 2025. Advocacy organizations say Canada is denying Afghan women and girls opportunities to study in Canada, despite a Taliban ban that bars them from pursuing secondary or higher education at home. (Sanaullah Seiam/AFP/Gett

blocks.text: After four years of being banned from the classroom in Afghanistan, a Kabul teenager was elated to win a full scholarship to a Canadian university prep school. Then her dreams came crashing down.
CBC is withholding the young woman's name for fear she could face retaliation for pursuing an education in defiance of Taliban law.

She was one of three Afghan teens selected out of thousands of applicants for a Canadian charity's education program. Then, in April, she was offered a two-year admission at a private boarding school in B.C., all expenses paid.

"When I first got my acceptance letter, my mind had made an entire new map, a new vision for me that could lead to my future," the 18-year-old old As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal. "I knew that all of my efforts had paid off."

But just a few months later, her hopes were dashed when Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) denied her study permit. Despite her full-ride scholarship, IRCC cited an inability to pay tuition among its reasons for rejecting her application.
IRCC declined to comment on the woman's case, citing privacy.
LISTEN | Interview with Kabul woman denied Canadian study permit:
As It Happens6:59An Afghan teen won a full scholarship to a B.C. school. But Canada denied her study permit
Her story is not unusual, say immigration advocates.

Multiple organizations told CBC that Canada has made a habit of rejecting study permits from Afghan women and girls, including those who have full scholarships, despite the fact that they face some of the strictest barriers to education in the world.
Advocate says gov't ignored scholarship

The Kabul student's scholarship was arranged by the non-profit Women Leaders of Tomorrow (WLOT), which partners with B.C. secondary schools to offer education opportunities to Afghan girls through its Empowering Limitless Minds program.
Of the three girls selected for the program this year, WLOT says two have been denied study permits, while the third remains in limbo.
WLOT executive director Friba Rezayee, a former Afghan Olympian, called the rejections "shocking."
She blames the Liberal government for reducing the number of international students it accepts to in 2024.

"The government has always said that they are standing in solidarity and support with Afghan women and they support human rights, democracy, and rule of law, and they also support girls' education," she said. "Then they deny their study permits."

Friba Rezayee, who is from Kabul, is the executive director of Women Leaders of Tomorrow, which arranges scholarships in Canada for Afghan girls to continue their secondary education. (Daryl Dick/The Canadian Press)
Rezayee says she believes the government is rejecting applications without thoroughly reading them.

In an IRCC letter to the Kabul teen, dated July 22, a case worker says the government denied her application, in part, because it was not convinced she would return to Afghanistan at the end of her stay, and because she had "insufficient funds/resources" to cover her tuition and cost of living in Canada.
But according to an April 27 acceptance letter from the B.C. school, she was granted a scholarship that covers tuition, school supplies, room and board, personal expenses and more.
"So they didn't even look at that," Rezayee said.

items: Girls are banned from Afghan schools. Secret networks are teaching them anyway

blocks.text: In an email to CBC, IRCC said all study permit applications "are considered on a case-by-case basis" based on the information provided.

It added that IRCC officers "examine files holistically" to determine "if they meet all program eligibility/admissibility requirements and if, on a balance of probabilities, the applicant is likely to respect Canada’s immigration laws and regulations."
There's still hope, says immigration lawyer
Immigration lawyer Gabrielle Thiboutot, who is not involved in the Kabul woman's case, says it's very plausible her application was not thoroughly vetted.
She noted IRCC uses automated software called Chinook to assess applications, and it could have missed the scholarship information.
CBC has asked the IRCC for information on how Chinook works and whether it could miss pertinent information.
Laurier grad is hoping her story will shine a light on education for girls in Afghanistan

Thiboutot sits on the board of directors for the advocacy group For The Refugees, which has run into similar roadblocks as WLOT. In 2024, two women the organization worked with were denied study permits to Canada, including one who had secured a $75,000 scholarship to Wilfrid Laurier University.

She says the IRCC argued the students would not return to Afghanistan at the end of their studies. This, despite that Parliament’s special committee on Afghanistan recommended in 2022 that the federal government issue study permits for Afghans with full Canadian scholarships “without assessing the intention of returning to their country of origin.”

But Thiboutot says For The Refugees successfully challenged the denied applications in federal court by arguing that even if the students don't go back to Afghanistan, their Canadian diplomas would open up opportunities for work or further study around the world.
She encouraged the prospective Kabul student not to give up hope.
"All the students we took on have arrived now," she said. "She won't make it for the semester … but the 'no' is not an end to her chance to come here for her studies."
Rezayee, however, says WLOT doesn't have the budget for a years-long legal battle.
"This message is directly to the prime minister, to Mark Carney," she said. "I need your attention on Afghan girls."
'It's not just about me anymore,' says scholarship teen
Speaking to CBC Radio from Kabul, the rejected applicant says this isn't the first obstacle she's had to overcome.
She still remembers 2022, when the Taliban banned girls in Afghanistan from attending school beyond Grade 6.
"I don't think I could ever forget," she said. "It was such a heavy moment."
Since then, she says, she's been taking courses in secret online. But she says the Canadian scholarship could be her last change to finish high school and carve out a better future for herself.

"I truly hope that they reconsider and review my application again," she said. "It's not just about me anymore. I have accepted this responsibility in my head to do this as a representation for all Afghan girls."

articles.title: Canadian military counterintelligence operative to face court martial in spy case
articles.summary: A Canadian military counterintelligence operative accused of sharing sensitive information with Ukrainian intelligence will face court martial beginning Dec. 9. Master Warrant Officer Matthew Robar…

image.caption: Master Warrant Officer Matthew Robar, a Canadian military counter-intelligence operative accused of passing sensitive information to a foreign entity, will face a court martial starting Dec. 9. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

A Canadian military counterintelligence operative accused of sharing sensitive information with Ukrainian intelligence will face court martial beginning Dec. 9. Master Warrant Officer Matthew Robar faces three charges related to unauthorized dealings with a foreign entity, misleading his superiors and improperly storing a firearm. He was originally charged with eight offences.
Master Warrant Officer Matthew Robar faces trial next month over alleged dealings with Ukrainian intelligence
A Canadian military counter-intelligence operative accused of passing sensitive information to a foreign entity will face a court martial next month.

Master Warrant Officer Matthew Robar, who had originally been charged with eight offences under the National Defence Act, will be tried on three counts beginning Dec. 9, the office of the chief military judge said in a statement on Wednesday.
He was accused of communicating "special operational information" to a foreign entity, which was not identified at the time of his arrest almost a year ago.
A CBC News investigation at the time of his arrest reported that he was accused of passing sensitive information to Ukraine.

The three charges Robar now faces include negligent performance of a military duty, claiming that between September 2024 and February 2025 he had "an unauthorized relationship with a foreign entity and shared unauthorized information with that person."
The second charge is prejudice of good order and discipline, where he is accused of lying to his superior officers about the extent of his dealing with the foreign individual.
He's also charged with improperly storing a firearm.

items: Operative accused of leaking secrets was trying to help Ukraine: sources
How a Canadian military intelligence operative ended up facing an espionage charge
Case started with claims that Postmedia journalist is linked to Russia: sources

blocks.text: The statement from the chief military judge did not explain why the prosecutor is not moving forward on the other more serious charges, including communicating special operational information to a foreign entity and one count of breach of trust.
CBC News has confirmed through confidential sources that the individual to whom Robar is allegedly to have passed sensitive information was a representative of Ukraine’s defence intelligence agency.
He was introduced to that individual by another Canadian official and it is that association which is at the heart of the case against him.

Confidential sources told CBC News last year that the allegations against Robar stem from a Canadian military counterintelligence investigation into claims that a leading Canadian defence journalist was a longtime Russian asset.
The sources said Robar was tasked to look into claims that Postmedia journalist David Pugliese had been recruited by the KGB in the early 1980s.
Those sensational allegations were made in public before the House of Commons committee on public safety on Oct. 24, 2024, by former Conservative cabinet minister Chris Alexander.
A dossier of records purportedly from old KGB archives in Kyiv were tabled with the committee by Alexander.
Pugliese, a hard-charging journalist with the Ottawa Citizen, has exposed wrongdoing and mismanagement at the Department of National Defence for years.

items: Military intelligence operative accused of lying to superiors over Ukraine contacts
Canadian military intelligence operative accused of leaking secrets released from custody
Canadian military intelligence member charged with espionage, says DND

blocks.text: He has vehemently and repeatedly denied the allegations, including in his own appearance before the same Commons committee in 2024.

In an interview with CBC News last year, Pugliese said no one in the Canadian military contacted him and he had no idea a counterintelligence investigation was underway. He also said the seven-page dossier tabled in Parliament contains a number of errors.

According to two confidential sources, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the investigation, the dossier on Pugliese’s alleged Russian intelligence ties mysteriously surfaced in Eastern Europe in 2023 and Ukraine intelligence's directorate (DIU) was handed a copy.

Nothing in the dossier proves that Pugliese carried out any assignments for the KGB, the predecessor of the FSB, Russia's modern-day intelligence service — or that he was even aware of the apparent Soviet interest in him.
An independent researcher, who claims to have been fascinated by the case, produced a separate report, which claims the allegations against Pugliese were fabricated.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.

articles.title: Code orange declared at hospitals in Prince George and Mackenzie, B.C., after major bus crash

blocks.text: Code orange declared at hospitals in Mackenzie, Prince George
Police say multiple people have been injured in a bus crash on Highway 39 south of Mackenzie, a small community about 160 kilometres north of Prince George.
Northern Health says a code orange has been declared at both the local Mackenzie hospital and the University Hospital of Northern B.C. in Prince George in relation to the crash.
A code orange designation is declared for disaster or mass casualty events, and the term casualty applies to both injuries and deaths.
The health authority said it still doesn't have details to share on the number of patients or their conditions.
Health officials are asking people in Mackenzie and Prince George to avoid going to the hospitals’ emergency departments unless they are facing a life-threatening emergency.
The public has been asked to avoid the area of the crash, and Highway 39 is expected to be closed for several hours.

articles.title: National chief didn't mean to 'hurt anybody' with remarks on Métis identity

image.caption: Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak maintains 'pretendianism' — people falsely claiming to be Indigenous — is a widespread issue. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New

The national chief who came under fire for her comments on Métis identity last week says she didn't want to "hurt anybody" but maintains there's a widespread issue of people falsely claiming to be Indigenous across Canada.
'You should be able to trace yourself back to First Nations people,' Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak maintains

When asked about the idea of abolishing the Indian Act on Oct. 26, Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said there's "a big group" of Métis people who "probably have First Nations roots" in Canada.
First Nations need control over who can claim membership, as the federal government has had too much say for too long, the national chief said.
"There's a lot of confused people out there who are claiming to be Indigenous, a lot of pretendians, and then a whole group of everybody else who says, 'I'm Métis,'" she said.
"Can you trace yourself back to a First Nation?"

Métis leaders condemned the remarks, including Manitoba Métis Federation President David Chartrand, who called them "racist," as the Métis are included in Section 35 of Canada's Constitution, which recognizes and affirms Aboriginal rights.
CBC News asked Woodhouse Nepinak on Tuesday about Chartrand's response and whether she felt she misspoke.

"This is bigger than a Manitoba issue," she said. "This is a Canada-wide issue, and I think there is pretendianism, and there [are] box-checkers in educational institutions, in governments, in government contracting, in business development."

items: Infrastructure gap and specific claims top issues for Assembly of First Nations for federal budget

blocks.text: The national chief said Canada created the issue and must "rectify the wrongs" caused by the Indian Act, which dictates who is classified as a status Indian, as well as Bill S-2 — proposed federal legislation that would end the second-generation cutoff for Indian status eligibility.

Decried as "legislative extinction" and "definitional genocide,” the second-generation cutoff blocks children from acquiring Indian status when two consecutive generations of parents have a partner who is non-status.
"Deal with all of those issues first, on lands and the issues of membership with First Nations, before trying to dovetail into other groups of people in this country," Woodhouse Nepinak said.
The national chief said she did not intend to cause harm with her comments last week.
"It's the truth that there's a big problem in this country with identity and identity issues, with certain groups of people," she said.
"You should be able to trace yourself back to First Nations people…. I'll leave that there."
Indian Act discussion 'sideswiped' other issues

The national chief's initial remarks came as First Nations leaders and Canada's first ministers met to discuss Indigenous rights for the first time in two decades. During that meeting, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew called for the Indian Act to be abolished.
On Tuesday, Woodhouse Nepinak also disputed claims by Kinew and Prime Minister Mark Carney that the idea to change or abolish the Indian Act was raised and supported by some chiefs in the room.
"No one" else brought up abolishing the Indian Act during the landmark meeting, the national chief said.

The chiefs involved had spent weeks preparing for the meeting and were focused more on the major projects legislation they say threatens their rights, but those conversations "went to the wayside" when Kinew and Carney made their remarks, she said.
"Those conversations can't be sideswiped just on one bombshell," Woodhouse Nepinak told reporters during a media scrum in Ottawa on Tuesday.
With files from Creeson Agecoutay and The Canadian Press

articles.title: Serbia detains police officers over alleged use of force against protesters
articles.summary:
Interior ministry claims suspects tortured and intimidated protesters detained in garage of government compound

Serbian authorities detained nine active police officers and one former…

blocks.text: Serbian authorities detained nine active police officers and one former officer on Wednesday for ⁠allegedly using excessive force against detainees during anti-corruption protests last year in Belgrade, the country’s interior ministry ⁠said.

Anti-corruption protests swept ⁠across Serbia, ​a candidate for European Union membership, in 2025 and 2026 after 16 people died when a concrete canopy ⁠on a renovated railway station in the city of Novi Sad collapsed on 1 November 2024.

The protests ultimately ⁠resulted in the ouster of the populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which is ​loyal to former president Aleksandar Vučić, in ‌an 25 October ‌snap parliamentary election by the leaderless Student List.

The ministry said in a ‌statement that the suspects, who served in an elite unit, tortured and intimidated several people detained in the garage of the government compound in downtown Belgrade on 14-15 August 2025.

“By the use of force and threats, (they) inflicted great pain and severe suffering on a larger ‌number of persons, intending to obtain information from them and intimidating and unlawfully punishing them,” the statement said.

The ministry provided ​only the initials of the officers and former officer who were detained. The news marked the first big arrests in connection with violence against the protesters who took to the streets over the past two years.
Police ⁠used teargas, crowd-control vehicles and stun grenades to disperse ​crowds during the ​protests.
Dozens of students and activists ​who took part in the protests accused police of ​excessive use of ‌force that ​resulted in injuries ​and psychological trauma.

Serbian students, activists, opposition politicians and rights watchdogs have accused Vučić and the SNS of political violence, pressure against media, ties to organised crime and rampant corruption. Vučić and his allies deny the accusations.

articles.title: Winners, losers, the EU: Five takeaways from the US midterms
articles.summary: Donald Trump's Republicans suffered a crushing defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, with the Democrats wresting control of Congress. What does this mean for US politics and the world?

image.caption: Donald Trump's power has been diminished now that the Democrats control CongressImage: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

blocks.text: The Democrats not only made significant gains in Tuesday's midterm elections but also took control of both chambers of Congress. Here are five insights that can be drawn from this moment.
1. US democracy is alive and well

The storming of the Capitol, attempts to change the rules of the electoral process, a spate of presidential executive orders to bypass Congress and many more examples sparked concerns that the US' vaunted democracy was being transformed into an authoritarian system under Donald Trump. But the country's democratic institutions have proven more resilient than many had feared.
Many voters were driven by their opposition to Trump's desire to rule with unfettered power. Instead they want to see country's institutional safeguards strengthened.

A post-election survey by news agency Associated Press found that about 30% of voters thought the state of democracy was the country's biggest problem. About 70% felt that Congress was not doing enough to provide checks and balances on the president.

This midterm result sends a clear signal that voters want stronger parliamentary oversight. President Trump could of course continue trying to govern through executive orders, bypassing Congress. But Congress sets the budget.

This means the Democrats, who now control Congress, can deny the president the funds he needs for his political initiatives. They can also set up investigative committees, which puts the Trump government under considerable pressure to justify its actions.
2. The Democrats can still win elections

For a long time, the Democratic Party lacked compelling leadership, a unified approach and a clear answer as to how it intends to win votes. Tuesday's election proves the party is still a political force to be reckoned with.

Its gains in many Republican strongholds are nothing short of sensational. The party was even able to score victories in Texas and South Carolina. In Kansas, the Democrats won a Senate seat for the first time since 1932.
The midterms have also put the spotlight on a new generation of Democrats: Younger politicians, some of them noticeably more progressive, who could chart a fresh course for the party.

Take, for instance, the Democratic Socialists of America, or DSA, an organization which is considerably more left-wing than the Democratic Party itself. At least five candidates endorsed by the DSA have been elected to the House of Representatives.

blocks.caption: James Talarico becames the first Democrat to win a Senate seat for Texas Senate in over 30 yearsImage: Eric Gay/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The DSA advocate for strong welfare policies that focus on affordable housing, health care and workers' rights. They also want to see greater checks on the power of large corporations.

"The argument was always that these folks can't win on a national stage," Brandon Bohrn, an expert on trans-Atlantic relations at the Bertelsmann Foundation, told DW. Now some of them have defied the odds and actually won, potentially sparking an internal debate about what the Democrats stand for and how they plan to win voters in the 2028 presidential election, Bohrn said.
3. The Republicans face a fierce internal battle over the party's future
Donald Trump has already made it clear that he does not hold himself responsible for this midterms defeat, taking to Truth Social to deflect any blame.

Yet not everyone in the Republican party is likely to agree. Critics of Trump who had been sidelined may feel emboldened to speak up again. The question as to whether the Republicans should abandon Trumpism will be almost impossible to ignore.

By law, Donald Trump cannot run for a third term in the 2028 presidential race so Republicans will have to think about who can. But who will take the lead? And more importantly: On what policy platform?
Tuesday's election defeat will likely accelerate this debate, making a power struggle over the Republicans' political future inevitable.
4. For Iran's leadership, Trump's defeat is good news
The war against Iran and resulting economic hardships have cost the Republicans many votes. The cost of living, in particular, was a key issue for many American voters.
The consequences of the Iran war have primarily driven up energy prices. This is likely to significantly increase domestic pressure on Trump to reach a lasting agreement with Iran.

Trump does seem keen to cut foreign policy costs, especially in areas where it has been politically controversial for his party. Shortly before the midterms, he announced that he no longer intends to provide billions in military aid to Israel. This was in relation to a deal that was meant to expire in two years anyway.
5. What the election outcome could mean for Europe

Ian Lesser, an expert on US foreign and security policy at the German Marshall Fund, believes that the midterm elections could also impact trans-Atlantic relations. "This actually makes a big difference for Europe in a number of different important ways," Lesser told DW.

blocks.caption: Trump has not shown great enthusiasm for NATOImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: The Democrats could try to reinvigorate dialogue between Europe and the US, Lesser suggests. After all, with control of Congress, the Democrats have more say on Trump's NATO policy, can influence budget decisions and military funding, and can complicate planned cuts to US support. Europe and the US may even cooperate on climate and environmental issues.
"Simply restoring a degree of trust and predictability, however we get to that, makes a big difference," Lesser said.
Not all differences will be resolved overnight though.

"Tariffs are a little tricky because there are clearly vested interests in the US in keeping some of this in place," Lesser concluded. "But in terms of new and very aggressive tariff measures, I think Congress would absolutely push back against that, on both sides of the aisle, actually."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Mother and daughter both killed in grizzly bear attack, Canadian authorities confirm
articles.summary:
Conservation officers say the women reported missing over the weekend, were found near a trail near their home

Search teams in Canada…

blocks.text: Search teams in Canada have discovered the body of a 20-year-old woman and confirmed that both she and her mother were killed in an attack that conservation officers now believe could have involved multiple grizzly bears.
Late on Tuesday, conservation officers in British Columbia said the two women, who were reported missing over the weekend, were located near a trail a short distance from their home.
The discovery has shaken a community where, earlier in the year, a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and their teachers.

“Our thoughts are with the families of the victims during this tragic time,” inspector Jeff Tyre said in a video posted online. Tyre later said the conservation service is probing the possibility that more than one bear was involved in the fatal attack.
“We appreciate people’s concerns and the desire to assist but it is critical the public stay out of the area – both due to the danger and to allow officers to do their work,” he said.

Jenny Balcarras, an art therapist, and her daughter Selah Reed were reported missing by relatives over the weekend. A family member posted on Facebook about them, later updating it after the conservation service announced the suspected attack to indicate that their vehicle had been found at a trailhead near Bella Coola, British Columbia. Balcarras’s remains were found first and Reed was located a day later.

A fundraiser for Balcarras started by her family mourned a woman who had recently moved to Bella Coola, a community of roughly 2,100 people, for a new job and “to start a new chapter” of her life. She leaves behind three adult children and a grandchild.

“[Jenny] was working toward building a future and had not yet had the opportunity to establish savings or put aside funds to help her family with unexpected expenses such as these,” wrote relative Mary Melissa Smith. “Tragically, no one could have anticipated that her family would be faced with such an unimaginable loss.”
The family also mourned 20-year-old Selah, who had her “whole life ahead of her” before the attack.
“She was only beginning her journey into adulthood, making this loss even more heartbreaking,” wrote Smith.
Both Balcarras and Reed had lived in communities in remote and rugged parts of the province, as well as time in Alaska.
The suspected attack happened at the Snooka West trail area, about 8km (4.97 miles) east of Bella Coola, on the province’s central coast.

Bella Coola, which sits at the end of a fjord along the province’s central coast, is a remote location, and abundant food sources mean that grizzly bears are a common sight in the region, which is informally known as the Great Bear rainforest.

Grizzly attacks in the province are exceedingly rare, but last November, 11 people, some as young as nine years old, were injured when a grizzly emerged from the forest near 4 Mile, a Nuxalk community, and attacked a school group on a lunch break alongside a walking trail. Despite an extensive search, the bear was never located.

Samuel Schooner, elected chief of the Nuxalk Nation, said on Tuesday: “Our thoughts are with the victim’s family as they learn of this tragic event.” Schooner said a trapping effort to find the bear was under way and asked media to refrain from contacting community members.
The province’s premier-designate, Lorne Doerkson, called the news “heartbreaking” and said he was thinking of the victims’ family and the Nuxalk Nation.
“At a time of such profound grief and uncertainty, my thoughts are with everyone who is hurting and with all those supporting one another through an incredibly difficult day.”

articles.title: 36 years later: Hungary opens Communist-era secret service files
articles.summary: Decades after the end of Soviet rule, Hungary is releasing all its secret service files. The disclosure is sparking fresh debate about informants, guilt and responsibility.

image.caption: Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar made releasing the documents a campaign pledgeImage: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP

blocks.text: On November 4, 1956, tens of thousands of Soviet soldiers and tanks swept into Hungary, brutally suppressing the country's anti-Communist uprising. Decades of dictatorship followed, relying on Hungary's brutal secret police to keep the system in place.
Events on Nov. 4 this year represent something of a reckoning with this dark chapter of Hungarian history.

Prime Minister Peter Magyar's government is ordering the full release of the country's secret police "agent files," which contain the names of Hungarian state security informants, some of whom cooperated out of their own volition even as others passed on information unwittingly.

blocks.caption: In 1956, Hungarians tried to stop Soviet tanks with cobble stone barricades Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Magyar and his Tisza party had previously promised to make the "agent files" public if elected. Their release is an historic event, as it comes after over three decades of heated debate over how to handle such sensitive files. The decision to publish is also sure to spark further debate on Communist-era guilt and responsibility.
Release opposed for years

Hungarians have been calling for the release of the files for years. After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the end of Soviet rule, civil rights activists and smaller Hungarian political parties said the files should be released. Demands for their publication were expressed repeatedly over following decades.

Yet Hungary's first post-Communist prime minister Jozsef Antall, a conservative, rejected the idea as did Viktor Orban's long-ruling Fidesz party. The latter blocked efforts to open the files, voting more than 30 times against such plans since 2010, according to Hungarian news platform Telex.

A partial release of state security files did occur in the 1990s, when the Hungarian parliament passed the so-called "agents law" in 1994. This required members of the government, members of parliament and certain public servants to undergo background checks to determine whether they had ever worked for the former state security services.
From 1997, Hungarian citizens have been able to view their own files and in 2003, permissions were expanded. But they have never been able to find out the names of informants.

The law relevant to the files contained provisions that were open to broad interpretation, which allowed government agencies such as the Ministry of Interior to prevent the transfer of files from the secret police to the Historical Archives of the Hungarian State Security, or ABTL, if they believed it would compromise national security.

Such a selective release of files not only prevented Hungarian society from learning the truth about its state security service, it also made it possible for files to be exploited in political power struggles, for example, by leaking compromising information about politicians to the public.

blocks.caption: Viktor Orban's Fidesz party never supported making the 'agent files' publicImage: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: One such case involved former Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Medgyessy, who was exposed by the Fidesz-affiliated daily Magyar Nemzet in 2002 for having worked as a Communist-era secret agent.
Political fallout expected
Magyar's government is putting an end to this. From Nov. 4, databases containing all the names of, and key information about, informants will be made available online.

Additional databases will be released as well. They include one of the most extensive databases on individuals recruited to work for the Hungarian state security agency. Confidentiality provisions set out in the old "agent law" have also been scaled back, meaning significantly more files will likely be accessible in the future.

The upcoming release of data on up to 60,000 out of an estimated 150,000 secret police informants could have major political consequences. Even so, ABTL director Bendeguz Gergo Cseh recently cautioned that, "you can't believe everything the state security agencies and their files claim." Many documents were incomplete and not fully reliable and many files had been destroyed, he said.

Others are also skeptical about the release. Historian Janos M. Rainer, an expert on Hungary's dictatorship, told Telex that the publication would have made sense right after the fall of the regime. Releasing the files after all these years is more of a symbolic gesture, he argued.

Meanwhile historian Krisztian Ungvary, who has researched the state security files extensively, welcomes the upcoming publication. It will allow historians to pursue new research and society to engage in fresh debates, Ungvary told DW. He believes Hungary will benefit from such reflection, as "societal lies inevitably lead to a strained relationship with politics and the price we paid for that was 16 years of Fidesz rule."

blocks.caption: Defendants are questioned by a judge in Budapest on March 9, 1957, during the first show trial held after the 1956 Hungarian uprisingImage: MTI/picture alliance

blocks.text: Political reckoning
For Magyar, making this information public carries great significance. The idea of coming to terms with the past, especially the years of the Orban regime, is one of his favorite topics.

When the Hungarian parliament amended the law about the files in mid-September, Magyar wrote on Facebook that, "after a 36-year delay, the Hungarian parliament today decided, at the initiative of Tisza, to make the 'agent files' public. Fidesz did not support the motion. I wonder why?"
It was an allusion to the fact that many prominent figures in Fidesz' ranks and in Orban's inner circle were members of the Hungarian Communist party or secret police.
The most well-known of the latter is likely Jozsef Horvath, a former full-time employee of the department of Hungarian state security that was responsible for suppressing the domestic opposition.

Under Orban, Horvath worked as an intelligence officer and security advisor, and in 2024, he became the research director of Orban's Sovereignty Protection Office. This was an agency that exposed supposed enemies of the Orban regime, branding them " foreign agents ."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: The midterms were a thumping rebuke of the US-Israel relationship
articles.summary:
Even Trump seems to recognize that the relationship has become a political liability, and may never be the same

On the eve of a midterm election that ended in an unequivocal rejection of his…

blocks.text: On the eve of a midterm election that ended in an unequivocal rejection of his brand of politics, even Donald Trump seemed to recognize that the US-Israel relationship has become a political liability.

Trump’s 11th-hour suggestion, on election morning, that he would cut military aid to Israel at the end of the year because, as he put it, “they don’t need it”, was condemned across the board – with pro-Palestinian advocates dismissing it as “desperate” and pro-Israel ones as “unserious”.

Trump’s suggestion that he would replace nearly $4bn in annual military aid with arms sales signaled little would change in practice – the funding would continue and it would be harder to track. But it was still a notable recognition by the president of just how much support for Israel has tanked against the backdrop of the latest war in Gaza, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinian, been widely been described as a genocide, and reshaped US politics in ways unthinkable just three years ago.

Indeed, come January, the US House will include an army doctor who went on a medical mission in Gaza, a lawyer who was fired by her firm over a blogpost criticizing Israel’s war, a Jewish lawmaker who was recently detained by Israeli forces while helping Palestinians harvest olives in the occupied West Bank, and a community organizer who participated in a pro-Palestine student encampment and scored one of the primary season’s most stunning upsets under the banner “babies, not bombs”.

Pro-Palestinian candidates – including Palestinian-American ones – have won downballot races. And in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim to be elected to the US Senate, following a campaign that saw more than $40m spent by Aipac in an effort to defeat him, last-minute drama, and unprecedented levels of Islamophobic rhetoric and bigotry.

“The old bipartisan consensus on Israel is over,” Beth Miller, political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, said. Without that consensus in place, the next Congress could push a number of measures, from an arms embargo on Israel to sanctions against violent settlers and officials – though Trump would retain veto power to block them.

The vote was also a rejection of Trump’s war in Iran – something even JD Vance said on Wednesday was “obvious to almost everyone”. Foreign policy issues rarely determine US elections – that is, until those issues have a direct effect on Americans’ lives at home.

“Americans were reminded of the failures of the Iran war with every visit to the gas station and grocery store,” said Yousef Munayyer, head of the Palestine/Israel Program at the Arab Center Washington DC. “Israel is a central piece of that story.”

Across the country, and up and down the ballot, unabashedly pro-Palestinian candidates defeated pro-Israel ones despite groups like Aipa pouring tens of millions of dollars into a failed attempt to reverse Israel’s collapsing standing among US voters. Last month, Aipac acknowledged its open support was hurting pro-Israel candidates more than it helped them, and announced it would stop making direct endorsements and contributions – a remarkable admission even if one with little practical consequence.

The victories of El-Sayed and several other candidates whom the right sought to cast as antisemitic over their support for Palestinians also marked a significant rejection of the narrative that pro-Israel voices and the Trump administration have relentlessly advanced over the last three years – that criticism of Israel is, by default, antisemitic.

“They try to call you hateful if you believe that Palestinian kids should get to grow up in the land of their forefathers without being murdered by our tax dollars,” El-Sayed, who has continued to speak plainly about his support for Palestinians despite coming under enormous pressure over it, said during his acceptance speech. “If you believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self determination, that’s not hate, it’s love.”

In Michigan, El Sayed won a majority of Jewish voters, according to exit polls. Despite warnings that Jews would leave the Democratic party en masse over its shifts on Israel, J Street said its polling found that 72% of Jews voted for Democrats on Tuesday, even though the Republican party increased its share of the Jewish vote since 2024..
This does not mean that the Democratic party is unified on Israel and Palestine and or in opposition to foreign wars.

For decades, the party has “excluded or marginalized anyone whose progressive values extend to support for Palestine”, Lara Friedman, the president of the Foundation for Middle East Peace, said . “American voters, organizers, and a cohort of enormously talented candidates came together and kicked the door down.”

Matt Duss, executive vice-president of the Center for International Policy and a former foreign policy aide to Senator Bernie Sanders, said that the Democrats now must seize the opportunity to become the party opposed to war.

“Trump ran and won as an anti-war candidate in 2024, because unfortunately Democrats left that lane wide open for him,” he said. “The question is: Will Democrats finally get it? Will they finally realize that Americans are tired of war and want a new foreign policy?”

articles.title: Kellogg's Rice Krispies changed its U.K. recipe, muffling its iconic snap, crackle and pop
articles.summary: Some consumers in the U.K. are in an uproar after cereal-maker Kellogg's recently changed its recipe there for Rice Krispies, replacing the whole rice grains in the family-favourite breakfast with…

image.caption: Kellogg's Rice Krispies cereal is displayed at a grocery store in 2025. Kellogg's swapped out whole rice for rice flour in the U.K. due to 'changing weather conditions.' (Mike Blake/Reuters)

blocks.text: Business

Some consumers in the U.K. are in an uproar after cereal-maker Kellogg's recently changed its recipe there for Rice Krispies, replacing the whole rice grains in the family-favourite breakfast with rice flour.
The cereal will continue to be made with real rice in Canada, Kellogg's confirms
This the way the world ends: not with a pop but a whimper.

This change is due to "changing weather conditions" affecting the quality and availability of rice, a spokesperson for Kellogg's in the U.K. told CBC News in a statement on Tuesday. The swap does not affect Kellogg's cereals in Canada or the U.S., another spokesperson for U.S.-based WK Kellogg Co. confirmed to CBC News.

"Our Rice Krispies cereals in the U.S. and Canada (e.g., Kellogg’s Rice Krispies, Kellogg’s Cocoa Krispies, Kellogg’s Frosted Krispies) are made with real rice and will continue to be," the spokesperson said in an emailed statement.
"There are no changes to their ingredients or recipes and consumers can continue to expect the same delicious Rice Krispies taste they know and love."

However, in the U.K., both Rice Krispies and Coco Pops now contain wheat gluten, making it unsafe for those with celiac disease or a wheat allergy. The change is reflected on the company's U.K. website, where the ingredients now include rice flour and wheat gluten.
The Canadian website still shows rice as the cereal's main ingredient, but also warns of barley and gluten as allergens.
Boxes of Kellogg's breakfast cereal are seen at a supermarket in Springfield, Pa., on July 11, 2025. (Matt Slocum/The Associated Press)
As many have noted, the recipe change also eliminated the iconic sound the cereal used to make when you add milk — a cornerstone of the brand's marketing for nearly a century.

"They've lost their snap, crackle and pop!" Susanna Reid, a co-host on Good Morning Britain, exclaimed after co-host Ed Balls poured milk over a bowl of the reformulated cereal on air Wednesday morning.
She held a microphone to the bowl. There was only silence.
"There's no snap, crackle or pop in these. My toddler won't eat them and she usually eats them every day," a person posted on TikTok.
"You can immediately tell the difference. They're soggy, pale, they don't have the snapping sound when you put milk in. It's really gross," someone else commented.
'The talking cereal'
Kellogg's Rice Krispies were first released in 1928, advertised as a "delicious cereal made from choice rice, cooked, puffed and toasted," according to the company website.

The words "snap, crackle and pop" first appeared in a print ad a year later, and have been printed on the cereal's packaging since 1932. The gnomes by the same name appeared in 1933 and made their television debut in 1955.
The cereal has been in the U.K. since 1928, Kellogg's pointed out in a 2018 press release, adding that it was marketed as "the talking cereal" due to "the sound it made when milk was poured onto it."
The rice grain fills with air when it's cooked, the company explained then, and when you add milk this forces the air to escape, creating the snap, crackle and pop.

items: These 5 grocery staples have skyrocketed in price this year. Here's why
How the Canada-U.S. trade war might change your shopping habits

blocks.text: The U.K. Kellogg's spokesperson says it recently swapped out the rice because it "helps us maintain consistent quality at a time when changing weather conditions are affecting the quality and availability of some of the rice and grains used in our cereals."
"We appreciate that even small changes to a much-loved product can feel noticeable and that’s why we have approached this with a lot of care and consideration," the statement continued.

The global rice crop is declining due to various weather issues in major producer countries, like reduced rain in India, El Nino-related disruption in Indonesia and drought in Italy, Europe's largest supplier.
The USDA predicts 2026 global rice production will fall 4.6 per cent compared to last year, reports industry news site Farm Progress.

articles.title: Fact check: Examining viral narratives after the US midterm elections
articles.summary: As Democrats celebrate major gains, false claims about election fraud have spread. Viral posts alleging illegal voting and election rigging are intended to fuel doubt about the integrity of the vote.…

image.caption: False claims circulating about election fraud fuel doubtsImage: Yuki Iwamura/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Democrats swept to victory in a closely watched US midterm election, delivering a strong rebuke to President Donald Trump and his Republican party.

At the same time, social media was awash with false claims that the election was fraudulent, including doctored screengrabs from media outlets, invented stories of illegal ballots and accusations of vote tampering.
Even as the votes are still being counted in some races, DW Fact check took a closer look at some election day disinformation.
Interpreters can help voters — contrary to fraud claims
Claim: "A highly coordinated scheme to steal an election is happening in real time," a right-wing media outlet claimed in a X post, viewed more than 700,000 times.

Attached was a security camera video showing a man helping voters at a polling booth in Lewiston, Maine, flipping through papers, marking ballots and speaking to them as they wrote. Other users in the thread claim they are Somali-American voters.

blocks.caption: CCTV footage has been used to allege voter fraud — without evidenceImage: x.com

blocks.text: Verdict: Misleading
Although the footage itself appears genuine, the claim that it shows a coordinated effort to steal the election is not supported by the available evidence.

Maine's election law says: "A voter who is unable to read or mark the ballot because of physical disability, illiteracy or religious faith may request another person ... to assist the voter in reading the ballot or marking the ballot according to the voter's wishes."
That hasn't stopped the right-wing account, The Maine Wire, the outlet that shared the video, from calling the practice a "blatant violation of state law."

The same account had been posting similar videos in the run-up to the elections. The outlet stated it had requested the footage from Lewiston City Hall under the state's own Freedom of Access Act. Authorities in Lewiston told DW Fact Check that it had denied a request for surveillance footage because ballots were visible in the recording and disclosure could violate Maine election law.
The Maine Wire reporters were accused of harassingSomali voters and recording people without permission.

The videos have been shared on Facebookand Reddit and a Trump-appointed federal attorney for Maine said his office would review evidence concerning complaints of voter intimidation and election interference.
The secretary of state's office told the local news outlet Maine Morning Star that it hadn't received any credible reports of interpreters committing election fraud.
The Department of Justice deployed election monitors to Lewiston and other jurisdictions ahead of the midterms as part of what it described as the largest election-monitoring effort in its history.
Fraudulent ballots not discovered by FBI in Houston

Claim: "Over twenty thousand fraudulent ballots uncovered in FBI raid of Houston storage locker warehouse all for Democrats" was the claim in a viral post on X that was viewed more than 400,000 times.

blocks.caption: Viral misinformation often recycles genuine images and links them falsely to unrelated eventsImage: x.com

blocks.text: Verdict: False
The Federal Bureau of Investigation confirmed that no such operation took place in a written statement to DW: "That information is false and no election-related operation occurred," it said.
The post's images also showed that the story was made up.

The first image, of an FBI truck at a crime scene, was taken from a different news story. A reverse image search reveals that the photo was taken during an FBI raid of the Fulton County elections warehouse in Georgia earlier this year, during which ballots from the 2020 election were confiscated. The truck has "FBI Atlanta" written on it.
The second image shows a storage facility in Houston. It was taken from the self-storage company Public Storage's website. There were no indications that an FBI raid took place there.
And the third image is an image of ballots with the words "city and county of San Francisco Department of Elections" printed on them, showing that there is no connection to an alleged raid in Texas.
The account that posted the story belongs to a man who calls himself a "Digital Content Creator for Pro Trump Administration TrumpNews.baby"
Doctored news reports misrepresent election reactions

Claim: "I cannot accept that the result tonight was free or fair. It is simply not possible for somebody with the radical ideology of James Talarico to win an election in Texas fairly" was the wording attributed to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in an X post designed to look like a still from the broadcaster NBC, which was viewed more than 700,000 times.

blocks.caption: Doctored reports from outlets are a common disinformation tactic

blocks.text: Paxton did not say this and this is not an authentic image of an NBC broadcast. In fact, the opposite is true: The Republican candidate for Senate conceded the race to Talarico.
"Let me start off by congratulating James Talarico. I will commit that I will be praying for him that he will do good for Texas and this nation," Paxton said to supporters at a campaign party.
Talarico won in a stunning upset, becoming the first Democrat to win a seat in the US Senate for Texas in over 30 years.

Republicans have been more likely to cast doubts on election results since Trump's failed attempt to challenge the outcome of the 2020 election. But Trump himself said he would acknowledge Tuesday's results.
How secure are the US midterm elections?
"I am absolutely willing the accept those results," Trump told the New York Times, in the days leading up to the midterms.

That wasn't the only social media post that used a doctored NBC graphic to spread falsehoods. Another viral X post allegedly shows the news outlets NBC’s 2026 election results with graphics and images claiming to show that Republicans won.

blocks.caption: The colors don't match the background colors used by NBCImage: x.com

blocks.text: Though it is a convincing fake at first glance, the graphics don't match NBC's normal background colors or shading.
Other users shared fake vote totals, too. This post, viewed 1.7 million times, shows doctored results with a Republican victory in Congress and the Senate.
'I had hopes, but this is unbelievable'
Alima de Graaf contributed to this report.

articles.title: Jimmy Kimmel roasts Trump in late night monologue amid 'blue tsunami' midterms
articles.summary: Late night host Jimmy Kimmel had some choice words for U.S. President Donald Trump last night as a “blue tsunami” stormed the country during the U.S. elections, quipping in the monologue of ABC's…

image.caption: Late night host Jimmy Kimmel mocked U.S. President Donald Trump in a monologue reacting to the midterm election 'blue tsunami' on Tuesday night. (Jordan Strauss/Invision/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Late night host Jimmy Kimmel had some choice words for U.S. President Donald Trump last night as a “blue tsunami” stormed the country during the U.S. elections, quipping in the monologue of ABC's Jimmy Kimmel Live! that Trump was "already running out of dipping sauce containers to throw at the television set."
Trump has repeatedly called for Kimmel to be fired by ABC
Late night host Jimmy Kimmel had some choice words for U.S. President Donald Trump last night as a “blue tsunami” stormed the country during the U.S. midterm elections.

Kimmel, host of ABC’s Jimmy Kimmel Live!, dragged the president through the verbal mud in his monologue Tuesday night, in a clip that has since racked up more than 8 million views as of Wednesday afternoon.
“Trump was reportedly angry and cursing as the results came in,” he said. “Word from inside the White House is he’s already run out of dipping sauce containers to throw at the television set.”
He added, “the blue wave made landfall, and now the Red Wedding begins,” referencing a famous massacre in the HBO show Game of Thrones.

No major late-night shows aired live during the election results, but Kimmel’s show was taped later in the night than usual, around 7 p.m. in Los Angeles, so that Kimmel could react to the early results.
And react he did.

“After all the talk about Nicki Minaj’s ass, John Husted’s ass, the only ass on Trump’s mind tonight is the one that just got handed to him,” Kimmel said, referencing Trump’s perplexing comments in recent weeks fixating on the gluteal physique of colleagues.
Jimmy Kimmel poses with the award for outstanding host for a game show for Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? during the Emmys in 2026, in Los Angeles. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)
“Democrats have officially taken the House, thanks to President Trump. Blob Vila flipped another house.”
The night saw Democrats retake the House and the Senate, winning several key races and flipping seats long held by Republicans.

Although the full results aren’t in yet, the Democrats have already gained seven seats in the Senate, 25 seats in the House, and five seats among governors, according to The Associated Press, making for a historic midterms for the U.S.
Leading up to the midterms, Trump frequently urged his supporters to “pretend I am on the ballot” in a bid to rally his base.

items: Trump strategy unchanged after Democrats' midterm landslide, says Canada-U.S. trade minister
Until the midterms, only 3 Black governors were ever elected in U.S. Tuesday saw 5 wins
What the Republican midterm defeat means for Trump, the U.S. and Canada

blocks.text: He struck a different tone on the phone to Fox News as the results came in, claiming that the sitting president always loses the midterms, and taking no responsibility for the Republican defeat.
“I shouldn’t feel guilty, because virtually … no matter how good the president is, you lose. I don’t know why. Nobody’s explained that,” he said.
Democrats seize control of U.S. House, Senate. What will they actually do?

He has blamed losses on lackluster candidates, even though Trump himself had endorsed or selected many candidates who suffered historic losses in areas long thought to be safe Republican seats. Trump hand-picked Darline Graham to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham as Senator in South Carolina, but she lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in an upset. Trump also endorsed Ken Paxton for Senator in Texas, only for James Talarico to make history as the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Texas in nearly 40 years.

“I have to believe he saw some of this coming, because this morning he was bragging about his approval rating in another country,” Kimmel said in his monologue, before playing a clip of Trump on Fox News talking about how he has a 99 per cent approval rating in Israel and joking that he’d move to Israel to become prime minister “if people ever get tired of me in the U.S.”
“That might be the best idea he’s ever had,” Kimmel said.
U.S. President Donald Trump walks from the podium after speaking at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on Monday in Washington. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

He slammed Trump for focusing on transgender people, “reflecting pools, racism against whites, Tylenol and Canada,” instead of priorities that align with “what Americans are worried about,” such as war, healthcare, climate change and inflation.

The Republicans’ historic losses come after an estimated $183 million US was poured into anti-trans attack ads attempting to criticize Democrats for supporting transgender people, according to The Associated Press.
Trump has repeatedly called for Kimmel to be fired by ABC in response to being the target of Kimmel's comedy.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

articles.title: Canada-U.S. trade minister says Democrats' midterm landslide doesn't change Ottawa's strategy

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump are seen together in June. Both leaders have said in recent days that trade talks are ramping up again. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Canada's point man on the Canada-U.S. trade file says the federal government's strategy isn't changing in the short term despite American voters handing a seismic win to Democrats in Tuesday night's midterm elections.
LeBlanc says Canada still must work with president and his cabinet

While the results are widely seen as a strong repudiation of U.S. President Donald Trump and his economic policies, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc wouldn't weigh in ahead of a caucus meeting on Wednesday morning in Ottawa.

"It's not particularly constructive for Canadians to interpret results in a foreign country's election," he said. "Our job is to focus on what we can control, and that's to work with the people that Americans have elected."
LeBlanc noted the trade talks are conducted with Trump and his cabinet.

items: Trump says it's 'largely true' Iran war led to Republican midterm losses

blocks.text: "They remain in office today. And those are the people with whom we'll be having those conversations," he said.
Canada has been seeking a trade deal with the U.S. in hopes of lowering steep tariffs on Canadian goods, including targeted sectors like autos, steel, aluminum and softwood.
'Our focus hasn't changed,' LeBlanc says as Democrats take U.S. Congress

One of the big questions for the Canadian side is how the infamously volatile U.S. president reacts to the midterm shellacking, one that delivered control of both the House and Senate to Democrats, and whether it gives Prime Minister Mark Carney's government more leverage.
Trump was already signalling some movement on the file, telling Fox News on Tuesday morning he was close to a deal.

Carney didn't go quite as far but told reporters that afternoon that the White House has shifted its stance on some of what he called Canada's "red lines," including language requirements and Canada's ability to strike trade deals with other countries.
'We've made progress' with U.S. on trade talks, Carney says
"They're asking less and they're offering more," the prime minister said, adding the two leaders will meet in China later this month.
He said there is still work to be done before a deal is inked. Autos are expected to be a key sticking point, as they were in August before talks collapsed — triggering new tariffs on both sides.
Trump still has his veto powers
A blue Congress doesn't necessarily mean it's clear sailing for Canada.
The new crop of representatives and senators won't be sworn in until January, and even after that Trump will still be able to lean on his executive authority.
After the results came Trump posted an image of a red MAGA-style hat with the word "VETO," although he also told Politico "I don't want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything."

LeBlanc said "what the new Congress might decide to do when they're seated two months from now is an interesting discussion," but that's "not going to change the work that we have to do in the next two weeks."
"The American Congress will act in the interests of the American Congress. Our work will be focused on what we can do here at home," he said.

items: What the Republican midterm defeat means for Trump, the U.S. and Canada
Carney says U.S. 'asking less and offering more' with 'more intense' trade talks underway

blocks.text: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said it's on Carney and his government to leverage the results to land a tariff-free trade deal with the U.S. administration.

"Americans hate these tariffs," he said. "Let's leverage that goodwill to pressure the administration and Congress to remove all the tariffs, lower the cost of living for Americans but also boost jobs and business for long-struggling Canadians."
Ford 'doing cartwheels'
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, one of the most colourful critics of Trump's tariffs at the premiers' table, said he "was doing cartwheels down the street" as the votes were being tallied.
"You ever seen a big guy like me doing cartwheels? I was jumping up and down when the results were coming in. But it's very simple, the American people spoke," he said.
Doug Ford 'doing cartwheels' over U.S. midterm results
Ford said he'll be reaching out to governors and is instructing his cabinet to reach out to U.S. Congress members and senators.
"The war is not over. We have to continue making sure that we move faster, quicker, immediate on everything across the board," he said.
Former ambo urging caution
Canada's former ambassador to the U.S., Kirsten Hillman, cautioned the federal government against making any sudden changes.

"If they're having constructive conversations that are heading towards some kind of arrangement that would work for Canada, we wouldn't want them to stop that," Hillman said during election night coverage on CBC News.
Former Conservative cabinet minister James Moore suggested Carney shouldn't accept a deal with tariffs now.

"Americans don't want tariffs. The polls and voters are clear. Do not make a deal with a repudiated and departing president that normalizes tariffs that Americans and Canadians don't want," he posted on X.
"Do not put Canada at an economic disadvantage with a tariff-accepting deal."

blocks.text: Manitoba
Connor Hellebuyck has posted a letter to Winnipeg Jets fans on his social media page, expressing gratitude to them, the organization and Manitoba's lakes.
Several factors went into trade request, including 'very challenging circumstances involving my family'

"I know my decision to request a trade was disappointing and frustrating for many people, especially those who supported me throughout my career. I understand those feelings, and I want everyone to know it was an extremely difficult decision," the letter says.
"I'll never forget the pride I felt representing Winnipeg, and I wish the Jets and the entire community nothing but the best."
The 33-year-old from Michigan spent his first 11 seasons in a Jets uniform before requesting a trade this past off-season and eventually being shipped to the New Jersey Devils.
His request left a bad taste in the mouths of many fans who took to social media to express anger and say good riddance.

items: 'I'm glad that he's gone': Winnipeg Jets fans say messy exit tarnishes Hellebuyck's legacy

blocks.text: There have been heated discussions online about the best Bronx cheers to offer Hellebuyck when he returns to Winnipeg with the Devils for a game on Nov. 10.
Jets fans are famous for having some of the loudest, wittiest, and most creative roasts.
Connor Hellebuyck posted this open letter to the Winnipeg Jets and the team's fans on social media Wednesday. (@hellebuyck.official/Instagram)

"When I think about my years in Winnipeg, I'll always be grateful for the life my family and I built there and for the people who became such an important part of it. It's where I grew as a player and where we started our family," Hellebuyck's post says.

"One of the things I've always loved about Manitoba is the connection people have to the outdoors. With so many beautiful lakes and places to enjoy nature, it's a special part of life there. Some of my favourite memories away from the rink will always be the time I spent on the water fishing."
There were several things that went into the decision to ask for the trade, "including some very challenging circumstances involving my family."
The family has chosen to keep those private, he wrote.

articles.title: What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress
articles.summary: Democrats can vote legislation through. But Trump still has veto power.

blocks.text: Election night was a fever dream for Democrats. In January, reality will set in.
They had a reason to be giddy on Tuesday night: Next year, Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress after a blowout victory.
"Today begins the great American comeback," an ecstatic Hakeem Jeffries, House Democratic leader, declared.

After months of promises on the campaign trail — to investigate corruption; lower the costs of healthcare, groceries and petrol; and curtail the Iran war — they will now begin the much tougher process of putting plans into action.

A shift in the balance of power in Washington doesn't necessarily mean Democrats will immediately get to start checking items off their legislative wish list. Democrats have Congress, but Republican President Donald Trump still has the power to reject legislation.
The Democrats should not consider what just happened "a mandate," US Senator Chris Coons told the BBC, warning that the party was still "deeply unpopular".
"We need to prove we can get stuff done, actually deliver answers to their concerns and questions about low wages and rising costs in particular."
Congressman Robert Garcia of California will soon lead a powerful oversight committee in the House, with the power to make Trump's last two years in office quite difficult.
"Lawyer up," the Democrat said in a statement as victorious results poured in on election night.

Committees in both the US Senate and House have investigative powers, which they could use to delve into alleged conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him. On Tuesday, Garcia rattled off a list of possible targets: Trump's family, "corporate corruption", alleged abuses by the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the government's handling of the Epstein files.
The Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations.

Should a US Supreme Court vacancy, for example, arise during Trump's term, Senate Democrats could use their new power to block a nomination - or force Trump to choose a more moderate candidate who garners bipartisan support.
The House also has the power to impeach a president - the first step of Congress' process to remove an official from office.

Democrats twice impeached Trump during his first term, though the US Senate eventually voted to acquit him in both cases. But because it takes a two-thirds majority in the US Senate — or 67 votes — convicting a president in an impeachment case likely will remain out of reach for Democrats.

There's an active debate among Democrats about whether impeachment is a good idea. The first impeachment, in 2019, unleashed partisan rancor and allowed Trump to cast himself later as a victim of political persecution, which later helped build support for his second White House run.
Jeffries, who would almost certainly have to greenlight any Democratic impeachment effort, has kept his plans vague.
"Well, we've made clear: We haven't ruled anything in," he told CNN in August. "And we haven't ruled anything out".
Americans' frustration with Congress' productivity was palpable before the election. Only 14% of US registered voters approved of lawmakers' performance, an October Gallup poll suggested.
But with a Republican in the White House and Democrats running Congress, Americans may face even more deadlock.

"If you thought legislating was hard in the last Congress with unified Republican control, that will get much more complicated," said Casey Burgat, professor of legislative affairs at George Washington University.
Because they will control both chambers with a comfortable majority, Democrats will be able to pass legislation through Congress with relative ease.
Getting it enacted into law will be harder.

A president must sign most legislation in order for it to become law. Trump has the power to reject legislation passed by Congress that he does not support, and Congress can only override him with a supermajority from both chambers - margins Democrats alone will not have despite their success on Tuesday.
As his party lost Senate race after Senate race Tuesday night, Trump struck a conciliatory tone with the New York Times.
"We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll, you know, look forward to working with them. We'll probably work something out," he said.

But a few minutes later, Trump posted a picture on Truth Social of his red campaign hat with the word "VETO" emblazoned across the front. That Jekyll-and-Hyde approach to a Democratic Congress could become a theme.
While opposition to Trump led to Democrats' success, lawmakers acknowledged Tuesday night, it might not be enough.
"It is overwhelmingly a rejection of Donald Trump, and his agenda and policies," Coons told the BBC.
"But if we overreach, or if we fight too much internally, we could miss this moment."

Despite the veto threat, Jeffries has said that his party wants to restore significant cuts Republicans made to healthcare programmes like Medicaid, which is used by low-income groups, and the Obamacare marketplace.
"We're committed as a top priority as House democrats to reversing these Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits," Jeffries said at a September event for healthcare workers.

On typically bipartisan issues – such as policies affecting affordability, regulating the AI industry, re-evaluating military funding for Israel and reining in the Iran War – talks could break down as lawmakers try to compromise. As they become the opposition heading into the 2028 presidential cycle, Republicans might not be in the mood to help Democrats achieve too many wins.

Fissures also could erupt even among Democrats themselves, particularly on matters involving Israel, that may make party consensus difficult. A schism emerged in the Democratic Party during the midterms over continued US military funds for Israel.

Incoming senators like Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, and some incoming members of the US House, said during the campaign they would vote for legislation to curtail aid to Israel. These Democrats could face a road block from their own leadership.
Then there's the matter of reining in Trump's foreign policy, which could be difficult, despite Democrats' majority.

Even before the midterms, Congress saw bipartisan efforts to limit Trump's ability to continue the war with Iran. Though some of these measures passed one or both chambers, Congress has not been able to enforce them. Notably, both the House and the Senate passed a resolution in June to halt hostilities with Iran, which Trump could not veto but has essentially ignored.

The White House has argued Trump has broad powers to continue the war. But Congress' authority to force Trump's hand is an "open legal question," said Scott Anderson, senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution.
"Congress can try to litigate this out, and force the courts to tell us."

articles.title: French blood banks targeted by refrigerator cyberattack
articles.summary: A cyberattack had attempted to destroy blood plasma by raising the temperatures in cold storage facilities past the boiling point.

image.caption: The blood bank was targeted around the same time as refrigeration systems at dozens of grocery stores in France and elsewhere Image: Maude Brulard/AFP

blocks.text: Blood banks in France were included among cyberattacks that hit refrigeration systems in several European countries on Sunday and Monday, French authorities said on Wednesday.
The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said that a "cybersecurity incident "targeted a refrigeration service provider affecting control systems at three cold storage sites for plasma and blood samples.

The cyberattack attempted to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but it was warded off before any damage could be done. The plasma in the affected refrigerators was transferred or secured, the EFS said.
"No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost," the EFS said in a statement, adding that its distribution operations were not interrupted.
Hackers try and make blood boil

The cyberattack was first reported on Wednesday by the French weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaine, which said the temperatures had been programmed to reach a boiling 110 C (230 F), rather than -30 Celsius (minus 22 Fahrenheit).
"Monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the anomalies, allowing staff to take action to ensure that no blood products or samples were compromised," the EFS said.
France's cybersecurity agency and Health Ministry said an investigation is underway, but did not indicate who could have been responsible.
The Health Ministry said Wednesday that remote access to the affected refrigerators was disabled, and credited monitoring and alarm systems with ensuring the safety of blood supplies.
Coolworld, the company supplying the refrigeration equipment, said the vulnerability was related to a component from a "third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld's direct control."
European supermarkets targeted by cyberattacks
On Sunday and Monday, a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at supermarkets in several European countries, including France and Germany, destroying large quantities of frozen food.
It was reminiscent of a similar attack three weeks ago targeting refrigeration systems at dozens of French supermarkets.
The attacks have cost supermarkets millions of euros in wasted food.
On Wednesday, Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize said it expects the cyberattack in October to reduce quarterly sales by as much as €250 million ($281 million).
"While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations," CEO Franz Muller said.

articles.title: Ukraine says bodycam video shows deadly Russian double-tap bombing
articles.summary: At least 40 people were killed and another 30 may still be under the rubble after Monday's attack on a Ukrainian village, Kyiv says.

blocks.text: The bodycam footage was released by Ukraine's national police on Wednesday.
It shows huge devastation after the first bomb strike on the village in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, as shocked local residents stare at the rubble.
Severely damaged buildings are also seen.
A voice of a military official is then heard on a two-way radio warning police on the ground of more glide bombs being launched towards Kamyshuvakha.
"Quickly [go] to the shelter!" one of the police officers tells local residents, who are seen walking into the shelter - at least two floors underground.
Seconds later the shelter is hit, and the recording stops.
Ukraine said the shelter was near a local school, which was being used to distribute humanitarian aid.
BBC Verify has confirmed the video was filmed in the same place as footage released by the Ukrainian state emergencies service DSNS showing the aftermath Monday's attack in Komyshuvakha.
In a post on social media on Wednesday, Zelensky said that "nine aerial bombs were dropped by the Russians.
"First, they hit people who came to receive humanitarian aid, and then rescuers and police officers who arrived at the scene."

The Ukrainian president added that "unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack", describing it as yet another of "thousands" of war crimes committed by Russia.
Ukraine's DSNS earlier posted another video showing a huge crater left after the attack on Kamyshuvakha.
The Russian military has not publicly commented.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Additional reporting Paul Brown, BBC Verify
