articles.title: Joy in Iran over ‘Trump’s defeat’ in US midterm elections – but war is not over
articles.summary: Iran celebrates its claimed role in ‘regime change’ amid pressure on US president to ‘finish the job’ with attack

blocks.text: Iran this week unveiled a massive new billboard and banners over Enqelab Square in central Tehran. The billboard pledged in English: “We will kill Trump” – elevating the degree of personal animus with which Donald Trump is viewed in official Iranian circles.

The poster depicts the US president behind bars with his head bowed. And in a sense, given the US midterm election results on Tuesday, Iran has indeed killed Trump, or at least the second term of his presidency. Trump’s reverse is all the more piquant because it comes on the day Iran’s leadership celebrates the anniversary of the seizure of the US embassy in Tehran in 1979, an event that ensnared Jimmy Carter, and a reminder of how Iran has ruined the prospects of more than one US president.
Not surprisingly, the keenly followed election results have led to a good degree of triumphalism inside Iran.

Ehsan Movaheidian, an international relations scholar, claimed: “The Islamic Republic of Iran has succeeded in regime change in America. The same will soon happen in Europe as well. Bow down before the power of Iran.”

Meisam Zohurian, a conservative member of parliament, said: “The joy over the outcome of the US elections has nothing to do with the arrival of this party or the departure of that party. The issue is the aggressor was smeared in the dirt and Iran had an impact on the result.”
Ali Nikzad, the first deputy speaker of the parliament, said: “These electoral defeats are the aftershocks of Trump’s defeat by the Iranian people.”

blocks.caption: A student walks over Israeli and US flags during a rally on Wednesday marking the anniversary of the 1979 takeover of the US embassy, outside the former embassy in Tehran. Photograph: Sobhan Farajvan/Pacific Press/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Iran’s supreme leader said anyone expecting a shift in US policy was “seriously mistaken”, however. “Those who still harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken,” Mojtaba Khamenei wrote.
Others predicted further electoral defeats for what they considered to be the warmongers in Europe, and the expulsion of US bases from the entire Middle East.

The resistance – or bloody-mindedness – shown by Iran for the past eight gruelling months did allow the strait of Hormuz to become an Iranian-controlled channel through which inflation and high diesel prices were transmitted to the American system. Even Trump himself on Wednesday accepted, and lamented, that the American people had decided the “short-term” pain of inflation was not a price worth paying to prevent Iran becoming a nuclear power.

But the big question now is whether either side will regard these seismic results as a moment to review their diplomatic strategy. Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, was quick to call on Trump to accept the wisdom of the American people. On social media he urged Trump to bow to the verdict of America: “Whether driven by conscience or the cost of living, America said no to war and we endorse this message.”
Ghalibaf added: “If the US government betrays the public will in order to serve international paymasters and blackmailers it will learn our ‘no’ comes with a nightmare.”

Yet Iran will also be asked to reflect on the wisdom of war by the Gulf monarchies, and possibly by Russia and China – the latter a country that seems finally to be stirring itself to find a solution to the blockade in the strait of Hormuz that is preventing badly-needed Middle East oil exports from reaching its industries.

China tends to knock only on doors that it knows are going to open, so it is probably testing the feasibility of a deal in which Iran “downblends” – or dilutes – its stockpile of highly enriched uranium inside Iran under international supervision. A Chinese special envoy is travelling to Oman, Iran and Saudi Arabia almost immediately.

These countries, some sympathetic to Iran’s predicament, can point out that if Tehran ever thought in the run-up to the elections Trump would capitulate and turn his carrier fleet around, it was mistaken. Some Iranian diplomats had indeed hoped that the prospect of defeat in the midterms, and pressure from within the Republican party, would have led Trump to make concessions to Tehran.
after newsletter promotion

In fact, both sides and the chief mediator, Qatar, clearly did try to use polling day as a lever, but in the end neither side retreated. Trump, for once, was true to his word and refused to allow the darkening opinion polls to reduce his determination to keep Iran in his vice. Confined to a holding bay of “neither war nor peace”, Trump’s priority was to keep the oil price as low as possible by repeatedly suggesting a settlement might be imminent.

For the next two months before the new Congress convenes in January – so reducing his budgetary options – Trump has greater latitude, and little accountability. The damage to the Republican party has been done and cannot be undone.

Unsurprisingly the Trump influencers who advocated for the war in the first place are piling on pressure to strike again quickly. Laura Loomer wrote on X: “Time for President Trump to deal with Iran once and for all. Just do it, Nothing to lose now. Finish the job.”

But the credibility of Loomer and her like has been severely damaged: in February, she had advised Trump that regime change in Iran – “a little excursion” – could be as easy as knocking over the Maduro regime in Venezuela. Similarly, Benjamin Netanyahu is now touting intelligence showing that Iran is preparing to use chemical weapons. The ease with which the Israeli prime minister conjures up intelligence to justify another assault on Iran may by now have struck the White House.

Hillary Clinton, Trump’s old sparring partner, is one who thinks Trump will probably launch the long-delayed attack. She said: “I think he will feel trapped. He will feel angry and resentful and he will react aggressively.”

Having come so far, and paid so high a political price, Trump may in the next two months try to secure a legacy by finishing the job – however he defines that. He is convinced, as he told Fox News this week, that “Iran has very few missiles and drones left, and even less capacity to build any more”. He crowed: “We are dealing with total strength. We can end it any time.”
Unfortunately, such blithe optimism has been heard before.

articles.title: Leading ice hockey nations, sponsors oppose Russia's return
articles.summary: Ice hockey's governing body says the impact of a court decision forcing it to reinstate Russia presents "significant practical and sporting challenges." Several leading nations say they won't play…

image.caption: The Court of Arbitration says Russian teams can return to international ice hockey, but against whom? And where?Image: Maksim Konstantinov/Imago Images

blocks.text: The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) said in a statement on Wednesday that the impact of last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) decision requiring it to reinstate Russia to international play had been "significantly underestimated."

It added that it "maintains" its disagreement with the decision and that it remained "in dialogue with Member National Associations, organizing committees, host authorities and other key stakeholders to determine the best way forward."

Shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the IIHF barred its teams from competing in international ice hockey tournaments, citing security concerns. In last Friday's ruling, the CAS said that the IIHF's concerns were "not supported by sufficient evidence."

Wednesday's statement comes after two days of talks by the IIHF Council aimed at charting a way forward following Friday's CAS decision, which appears to have caught most of the international ice hockey community off guard.

Two of the organizing committees the statement refers to are those of Canada, which is due to host the IIHF World Junior Championship starting next month, and Germany, which is to host the IIHF Men's World Championship next May. Both countries are strong supporters of Ukraine in its war against Russia, and both have expressed serious reservations about their upcoming tournaments in light of the CAS ruling.
'Russians will not be in Canada'
On Tuesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ruled out allowing Russians to compete in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he told reporters at a press conference in Antigua, where he was attending a Commonwealth meeting.
"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

blocks.caption: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has ruled out Russian participation in the World Junior Ice Hockey Tournament in Alberta next monthImage: Jon Blacker/The Canadian Press/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Last weekend, Frank Lutz, chairman of the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) conceded in a television interview that following the CAS decision, the DEB would "also have to consider the option of handing back (hosting rights to) this championship."
Lutz was to discuss the matter with government officials in Berlin this week. A government spokesman said on the weekend that Berlin "takes a very critical view" of the ruling.
Growing European boycott of Russia
Meanwhile, the ice hockey association of Finland, the defending men's world champions, has been spearheading an effort to boycott upcoming IIHF tournaments should the Russians be allowed to compete.

"We are currently working to bring as many countries as possible into a united front to tell the IIHF that none of us will play against Russia under these circumstances," Finnish Ice Hockey Association boss Heikki Hietanen said in a statement released on the organization's website on Monday.
"Our stance is that we will not play against Russia as long as the war of aggression against Ukraine continues," added Hietanen, who is also a member of the IIHF Council.
Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Czechia have since made similar statements.
"The Three Crowns will not play Russia in coming world championship tournaments," Swedish Ice Hockey Federation boss Anders Larsson said.
This came shortly after Norway said it would not play Russia at the Men's World Championship and the Danish Ice Hockey Federation issued a similar statement on its website.

"Denmark will – based on the current situation and the information available to us today – not play against Russia at the World Championship in Germany in May 2027," it read. Denmark did not qualify for the World Juniors.
Czechia Ice Hockey Association President Alois Hadamczik confirmed on Tuesday that they too would refrain from playing Russian teams.
Latvia's federation said it “reaffirms its longstanding and firm position" not to play against Russia or its ally Belarus.
Alexander Helwig, chairman of the Austrian Ice Hockey Association told public broadcaster ORF that “as of now, we would certainly not play against Russia."
USA Hockey has yet to comment on the CAS ruling.

blocks.caption: The AJ Products and Skoda logos have long been a familiar sight at World Ice Hockey ChampionshipsImage: Richard Wareham/IMAGO

blocks.text: Sponsors having second thoughts

At the same time, sponsors of IIHF tournaments are also getting cold feet. Skoda, which has been the main sponsor of the Men's World Championship for more than three decades, told the Associated Press that it would "reassess" its position if Russia takes part.

"We do not support the Court of Arbitration for Sport's decision regarding the participation of Russian national teams in IIHF competitions. With Russia's aggression continuing, we believe the Russian national team's return to the world championship is incompatible with the values we have consistently upheld," the Czech carmaker said.

Skoda isn't alone either, Finnish tire manufacturer Nokian had said it would end its backing if Russia took part and Swedish furniture maker AJ Products, whose logo has been seen on the boards and officials' jerseys at World Championships since 1989, said Monday it would ask for its logo not to be shown.

With the IIHF Council having failed to agree on how to proceed during its meetings on Monday and Tuesday, President Franz Reindl told Germany's SID news agency on Wednesday, that it would reconvene for further talks on Thursday.

articles.title: US midterm elections 2026 live updates: Democrats take control of Congress in major setback for Trump
articles.summary: Democrats flip seven Senate seats in Kansas, Iowa, Texas, Maine, Ohio, North Carolina and South Carolina; ‘blue wave’ rejects Trump’s agenda

blocks.text: Democrats secure majority in the House as voters punish Republican Party
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

In case you fell asleep early, yesterday evening resonated as an extinction level-event for Donald Trump’s Republican Party, a worst-case scenario for the GOP that even the starkest polls might’ve underestimated.

Democrats defended a crucial Senate seat in Michigan and won the likely pickups in Maine and North Carolina. They then proceeded to flip five more seats in states that would normally be considered unquestionably red: Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina, and — the biggest prize of them all — Texas.

As of Wednesday morning, Democrats have secured 54 seats in the Senate. A closely-watched race in Alaska is yet to be called. And the Senate contest in ruby red Mississippi is down to the wire, with Democrat Scott Colom leading by just a few dozen votes as the final ballots roll in.

The Democrats have already secured 228 seats in the House, ten more than needed for a majority, and could realistically run up the score to 240 seats or more. They’ve also flipped governor’s offices in Texas, Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, and Nevada.
Republicans, needless to say, are shell-shocked, with the future of the party deeply uncertain, and some sounding the death-knell for a decade of Trump-dominated GOP politics.
Here are some other developments you may have missed last night:

items: Trump, uncharacteristically gracious, accepted his party’s resounding defeat, congratulated Democrats, and told The New York Times that he was “absolutely willing to accept” the election results. That was very much in doubt after the Trump administration spent months seeking to exert greater influence over the elections process through executive orders and the courts.

Deb Haaland, running in New Mexico, became the first Native American woman elected as governor. Keisha Lanca Bottoms became the first Black woman ever elected governor. Abdul El-Sayed, the victorious Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, became the first Muslim voted into the upper chamber.
Several key congressional races, including contests in Colorado, Michigan, Maine, New York, California, and North Carolina, remain to be called.

blocks.text: Key events

items: 17m agoDemocrats secure majority in the House as voters punish Republican Party

blocks.text: The results of a closely-fought California ballot proposal to impose a one-time tax on billionaires remain too close to call as of Wednesday morning, the Associated Press reported.

If it passes, the measure would hit the state’s ultra-wealthy with a one-time 5% tax. It prompted something of an internecine war among California Democrats, winning support from top progressives, but getting blowback from some party leaders including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who fear its passage would force an exodus of the state’s ultra-wealthy.
Those same ultra-wealthy have also spent lavishly to campaign against the proposal.

items: Trump, uncharacteristically gracious, accepted his party’s resounding defeat, congratulated Democrats, and told The New York Times that he was “absolutely willing to accept” the election results. That was very much in doubt after the Trump administration spent months seeking to exert greater influence over the elections process through executive orders and the courts.

Deb Haaland, running in New Mexico, became the first Native American woman elected as governor. Keisha Lanca Bottoms became the first Black woman ever elected governor. Abdul El-Sayed, the victorious Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, became the first Muslim voted into the upper chamber.
Several key congressional races, including contests in Colorado, Michigan, Maine, New York, California, and North Carolina, remain to be called.

articles.title: Indonesia deploys troops to Jakarta after wiretapping allegations
articles.summary: Indonesian troops are being stationed in Jakarta amid wiretapping allegations implicating the president's chief of staff. Suspects are being accused of illegally tapping the president's phones.

image.caption: President Prabowo Subianto's government has yet to determine the motiveImage: BPMI Setpres/Kris

blocks.text: Indonesia's military deployed more than 20,000 troops and personnel to the capital city Jakarta after authorities launched an investigation into an alleged wiretapping operation targeting the President Prabowo Subianto.
Some 20,000 troops have been deployed in Jakarta amid the scandal with the president's chief of staff is currently being investigated.
Senior military figures implicated
So far, three senior police generals have been detained. They are being accused of illegally tapping the phones of the president, journalists, politicians and business people.
Among those detained is Listyo Sigit Prabowo — not related to the president — who was the national police chief before becoming the president's chief of staff last month.
The presidential palace claims the alleged wiretapping targeting President Subianto could be regarded as an act "tending towards treason."
The authorities did not officially confirm that the deployment is connected to the scandal.
The number of troops and personnel deployed to the capital since Monday surpassed 20,000 as of Wednesday, according to the navy operations assistant, Vice Admiral Yayan Sofiyan.
Indonesian armed forces spokesperson Major General Muhammad Nas claimed that the troop movement was a "standart procedure" for maintaining national security.
Motive yet to be established
According to Indonesia's senior minister for legal affairs, the government has yet to determine the motive for the wiretapping.
The suspects, who have not responded publicly to the allegations, could face unlawful surveillance related charges, which can lead up to 10 years in prison.

"There is a strong suspicion that the wiretapping was carried out not in the interests of the state or the National Police, but for the interests of other parties,” Adrianus Meliala, a criminologist at the University of Indonesia and a former commissioner of the National Police Commission said.

"No one expected Listyo Sigit Prabowo to be named a suspect,” said Meliala, "But if the allegations are proven, the case could be understood in the context of political maneuvering. Anyone who engages in politics must also be prepared to face the political consequences," Meliala said.

articles.title: Israel’s election commission rejects Netanyahu claims of voting fraud
articles.summary:
Move comes after attorney general blocked Shin Bet call to interrogate politicians from Palestinian-led parties

Israel’s election commission on Wednesday confirmed the final results of the…
articles.byline: Emma Graham-Harrison and Quique Kierszenbaum in Jerusalem

blocks.text: Israel’s election commission on Wednesday confirmed the final results of the 27 October vote that stripped Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition of their governing majority, rejecting claims of mass fraud promoted by the prime minister.

His main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, warned that Netanyahu had launched a “pogrom against democracy”, attempting to hold on to power by discrediting valid votes and weaponising security forces against parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Hours earlier Israel’s attorney general said she had blocked a demand from the Shin Bet security service to interrogate senior politicians from the Palestinian-led parties, because she was not presented with any evidence of wrongdoing.

“In a country governed by the rule of law, neither citizens nor elected officials can be interrogated without evidence that justifies doing so,” Gali Baharav-Miara said in a statement, after Haaretz reported the attempt to target four politicians.
Election authorities on Wednesday presented the final results to the president, Isaac Herzog, after rejecting allegations they had been tainted by large-scale foreign interference and voter fraud.

blocks.caption: People take part in a rally in Tel Aviv calling for the opposition to form a government with the Arab parties after last week’s general election. Photograph: Jamal Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: “The review found no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results,” the Central Elections Committee said in a statement.
The body’s chair, Noam Sohlberg, added that some “suspicions” were still under investigation, but “they do not cast doubt on the election as a whole or justify delaying the election results”.
When the results were handed over Herzog also denounced racist attacks on Palestinian citizens, who turned out to vote at historic rates.

“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said. “I hold Arab society in Israel in great respect. I value its contribution to the country in every area of life, and its desire to integrate.”

Herzog plays a key role in formation of the next government, by choosing which politician has the first chance to create a coalition. He is expected to name Eisenkot, in an announcement that could come as early as Thursday evening.

A former leader of the Israeli military who lost his son fighting in Gaza, Eisenkot has secured the public support of all the Jewish Israeli opposition parties. Palestinian-led parties have said their priority is removing Netanyahu so are also expected to back him as the strongest contender to achieve that.

However, negotiations could take weeks and Eisenkot warned of ongoing attempts to undermine trust in the election results. He also accused Netanyahu of weaponising the security services against domestic opponents in a bid to hold on to power.

blocks.caption: Gadi Eisenkot has secured the public support of all the Jewish Israeli opposition parties. Photograph: Paulina Patimer/JNA/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “The employees of the Ministry of Defense, law enforcement, and the civil service in Israel are servants of the state, not the king,” he said in a statement. “Woe to anyone who abuses their authority and role for political considerations.

The Shin Bet chief, David Zini, handpicked for the role by Netanyahu, had ordered the interrogations and sought to classify the investigation as a security file, which would allow harsher conditions including barring the politicians from having legal counsel.
Analyst Nadav Eyal warned that Israelis should brace for more extreme attempts to dismiss election results and discredit the leading opposition parties.
“The groundwork is steadily being laid for violence,” he wrote on X. “What you’re hearing breaking right now is the foundation of the legal and governmental orders in Israel,”

Netanyahu presided over a racist campaign targeting Palestinian citizens of Israel, about 20% of the population, and on election day began promoting the unfounded accusations of mass fraud now rejected by election authorities.

Ahmad Tibi, one of the most prominent and effective Palestinian politicians, was reportedly among those the Shin Bet sought to interrogate. He responded to the latest allegations, as the news of sweeping victories for Democrats in the US midterms, with a swipe at Netanyahu’s fear of democracy.

“(The) Attorney General is checking suspicion of ties between the Joint List and Democrats in the US,” Tibi wrote in a social media post. “According to the suspicion, in both cases the same sophisticated method was employed: people arrived in droves at the polling stations, cast a slip, and went home.”

articles.title: BMW reports lower Q3 earnings as China woes mount
articles.summary: BMW reports a drop in profits in the July to September quarter amid fierce competition from China.

image.caption: BMW set to ramp up restructuring measures (File: September 2026)Image: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German carmaker BMW reported a nearly 15% drop in third-quarter pretax earnings on Wednesday, as competition from China shakes the global car industry.
Net profit for the third quarter fell to 1.45 billion euros ($1.61 billion), while sales fell nearly 6% to 30.45 billion euros, BMW said.

The main cause of the decline was BMW's poor business in China. Although the company sold more cars in the US and Europe compared to the same period last year, this could only partially offset the decline in China.
BMW's car deliveries in China, which were already at their lowest level since 2017 last year, fell 24.8% in the quarter and consequently dragged global deliveries down by 6.3.
CEO Milan Nedeljkovic said his company would "specifically intensify and accelerate structural measures."
Can crisis reinvent the car again?
The German carmaker lowered its outlook for the current year, citing the faster-than-planned implementation of restructuring measures that includes 8,000 layoffs in its home market.
Germany's auto industry struggling because of weak demand and competition from China
German carmakers have been struggling to compete with their Chinese counterparts in the electric vehicle market, resulting in cost-cutting measures.
Volkswagen, the world's second-largest carmaker, is battling mounting competition from falling demand in its core Chinese market.
BMW, and its industry heavyweight peers, Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs.
The legacy car industry is in crisis. How can it move on?
The Volkswagen Group posted its worst quarterly results in more than a decade earlier this October.

It is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW has announced that it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027.
On the other hand, German auto parts supplier Schaeffler announced on Tuesday that it planned to cut almost 3,500 jobs and close five sites in Europe, by 2028.
According to the company statement, three-fourths of the 3,460 job cuts and four of the five site closures will be in Germany.
German automotive supplier Bosch, the world's biggest, announced last year that it would cut 13,000 jobs, mostly in its auto division.

articles.title: Germany's celebrated children's author Janosch has died
articles.summary: Bear, Tiger and Tiger-Duck: The author and illustrator Janosch achieved world fame with his heartwarming children's figures. He died at the age of 95.

image.caption: Janosch standing next to his beloved characters, Bear and Tiger, in 2010Image: Roland Weihrauch/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Janosch, the pen name of German author and illustrator Horst Eckert, won hearts around the world with his warm and simple sense of humor. He charmed children and adults alike with his iconic Tiger, Bear, Tiger-Duck and other animals.
Janosch created more than 150 books, which have been translated into over 30 languages.

His best-selling children's book, "Oh, wie schön ist Panama," translated into English as "The Trip to Panama," was so lucrative that Janosch was able to settle down on the Canary Island of Tenerife in 1980, where he lived together with his wife Ines. The writer and illustrator died peacefully at the age of 95, his publisher Bernhard Feil announced on Wednesday.
Dismissed from arts school
Janosch was born as Horst Eckert on March 11, 1931, in Hindenburg (now Zabrze, Poland) in what was then Upper Silesia. After World War II, his family had to flee to Germany.
In 1953, Janosch started studying at the Academy of Art in Munich, thinking that it would be easy to become an artist. He was however dismissed after just a few terms for "lack of talent."

blocks.caption: This way to Panama: A sign in a bookstore featuring the author's famous illustrations Image: Uwe Zucchi/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: But luckily for his later readers, Janosch did not give up. He continued to work as a freelance artist, soon discovering his second great gift, namely writing.
His first children's book about a horse named Valek was published in 1960.
Although Janosch became famous primarily for his children's books, he also wrote books for adults that focused on his own childhood.
The dream of a beautiful childhood

Even though he wrote cheerful books for children, Janosch hardly had any positive memories of his own childhood, as his father was an alcoholic. He was beaten not only by him, but also by his mother and grandmother. Raised in a strictly Catholic environment, he was continuously threatened to be punished by God.
Later on, Janosch tried to overcome the burden of his childhood memories by turning to alcohol as well.

He always expressed a great deal of understanding for children, trying to encourage them to stand up for their rights. As a result of his childhood experiences, Janosch did not want to have children himself, and his attitude towards the Catholic Church always remained divided. "As I am a sinner and a heretic, God will let me live a long life so that I can return to the Church," he told his biographer Angela Bajorek.

Janosch's animal figures are endearing, but not always well-behaved. They love all kinds of nonsense. But even if they lie to each other or put their own interests first, the true winner at the end of stories is always friendship and solidarity.
Janosch's path towards world fame

Janosch achieved his major breakthrough with "The Trip to Panama," a story about two friends, a little tiger and a bear, who set out to find their paradise in Panama. After touring around in circles, they finally end up where they started out; they realize that their journey was the destination. Janosch received the German Youth Book Prize in 1979 for the work.
Janosch's protagonists have become familiar to generations of children all over the world. They come up over and over again in the various stories carefully illustrated with water colors.

blocks.caption: The author next to a poster of 'Janosch's Dream World,' which was a TV series based on his booksImage: Horst Galuschka/IMAGO

blocks.text: There is the honest lion Hans from the toy chest who fails to catch a nutcracker with his lies. There is Schnuddel and a ridiculous bragger Günter the Box-Frog. And then there is a tiger that collects mushrooms while looking out for his devoted friend, a bear, who always stands up for him even when the tiger temporarily leaves him because of a little pig in one of the stories.
Merchandising with a Tiger-Duck

The "Tigerente," literally "Tiger-Duck," a wooden duck on wheels with yellow-brown stripes, appears on numerous pictures by the illustrator. At times, the animal has been tossed into a corner, at times it is hanging from the ceiling, or the Box-Frog pulls it across the drawing.

His iconic figures, especially the Tiger-Duck, have served as motifs on various items, from cups to stamps to jewelry, and even on airplanes. Film adaptations and TV series based on his stories were produced in German and English.

blocks.caption: The Tiger-Duck character is a little wooden toy duck on wheels, with black and yellow stripes, shown here as a stuffed toyImage: Jörg Carstensen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'He who needs almost nothing, has everything'

Guests who visited Janosch in Tenerife were impressed by his very modest lifestyle. He always said that hanging around in his hammock doing nothing was what he enjoyed most. And yet Janosch remained very active until the end of his life.

From 2013 to 2019, he wrote a column for the German weekly Die Zeit, taking on the role of Mr. Wondrak, who commented on world affairs. Shortly before his 90th birthday in 2021, the complete collection of his Mr. Wondrak columns were published as a book in German.
Like the protagonists in his stories, Janosch always tried to content himself with few things. As he wrote in one of his books: "He who needs almost nothing, has everything."
This article was originally written in German.

With most eyes still on the US this morning, Brussels is quietly getting on with the task of leading on discussions about the next round of support for Ukraine.

articles.title: Ecstatic scenes and historic moments: What's happened so far in the midterms
articles.summary: Democrats have taken control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency - proving moments of celebration.

blocks.text: Ecstatic scenes and historic moments: What's happened so far in the midterms
How the Democratic takeover of the Senate could impact Trump
ByNardine Saad
Reporting fromLos Angeles, California
Democrats have won both the US Senate and House of Representatives, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
Even before results are finalised, the night has provided some historic results and scenes of celebration. These are some of the key moments so far.
Democrats talk of 'great American comeback' after historic results

Democrats have tallied up victories in states that were comfortably won by Republican President Trump two years ago, registering sizeable swings in the likes of Texas, Kansas, Ohio and South Carolina.

Among the senior party figures who have cheered the results are Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is now poised to take over as the speaker of the lower chamber of Congress.
"Today begins the great American comeback," he told a crowd of supporters.
If Jeffries' colleagues choose to keep him as the leader of their party's delegation in House, he will be the next speaker, taking over from Republican Mike Jeffries.
Trump congratulates opposition on 'good job'
Trump has spoken throughout the night to a number of media outlets, striking a conciliatory tone and conceding that the Democrats did a "good job".

He said he would accept the results and that he was looking forward to working with the opposition party - albeit he would still have the power, as president, to veto legislation that Democrats advance through Texas.

Trump distanced himself from some of the Republican candidates who contested the election, saying: "In some cases they didn't like the candidates, and in some cases those candidates were not my friend."
Cheers as Democrats win first Senate flip of the night in North Carolina

blocks.caption: Image caption, Roy Cooper was expected to have a tough fight on his hands in North Carolina

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Roy Cooper was expected to have a tough fight on his hands in North Carolina
There were cheers from supporters in North Carolina as the Democrats secured the night's first flip of a Senate seat.
The state's former Democratic governor, Roy Cooper, won against Republican candidate Michael Whatley.
"Tonight we show the country that when everyday people come together, we can make change," Cooper said as he addressed his supporters on Tuesday.
The last time the Democrats won a Senate race in the state was 2008, despite the party making enormous investment in time and money behind their candidates in recent contests.
Keisha Lance Bottoms becomes first black female governor

blocks.caption: Image caption, Keisha Lance Bottoms beat billionaire businessman Rick Jackson,

blocks.text: Keisha Lance Bottoms beat billionaire businessman Rick Jackson,

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, has been projected to win the governor's race in Georgia, becoming the first black governor and first woman to be elected to the state's highest office.
The BBC's Carl Nasman described ecstatic scenes as the race was projected blue, which came after the state's former senator said the party was "nauseously optimistic" about their chances this year.

Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire businessman and healthcare executive, who was endorsed by outgoing Governor Brian Kemp and President Trump, who spent $200 million of his own money on the race.
The state has also not had a Democratic governor in more than 20 years.
Ossoff victory in Georgia adds fuel to 2028 speculation

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jon Ossoff as seen as a potential future Democratic contender for the presidency

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Jon Ossoff as seen as a potential future Democratic contender for the presidency
As well as Bottoms being elected the new governor of Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff has been projected as the winner of the Senate race there, giving him a second term.
His victory was not unexpected as he had a comfortable lead in the polls over his Republican challenger Mike Collins - a member of the lower House chamber.
Ossoff told his supporters following his victory that for those who "doubted whether our republic would survive" over the last two years, the "first light of dawn is on the horizon".

Republicans had hoped this would be a more competitive race because the Peach State has been reliably Republican for decades. Trump also won it in the 2024 presidential election, after Joe Biden eked out a narrow victory there in 2020.

Now that he has won re-election in the Senate, the speculation surrounding Ossoff's plans for the next presidential election in 2028 will likely increase - he is considered a potential leading contender if he throws his hat in the ring.
Chris Pappas celebrates with husband as first openly gay man elected to Senate
Watch: "I am ready to fight" - Senator-elect Chris Pappas celebrates New Hampshire win
Democrat Chris Pappas has also made history as the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. He celebrated on stage alongside his husband in New Hampshire.
Pappas is projected to defeat former Republican Senator John Sununu in the race - who comes from one of the state's political dynasties having seen his father and brother serve as governor.

But the contest between the two was well-natured, with Pappas thanking his opponent on Tuesday by saying: "We all owe John Sununu a big debt of gratitude for his public service for the people of New Hampshire."
The 46-year-old Pappas had represented New Hampshire in the House since 2019 but chose not to run for re-election so he could launch his campaign for the Senate.

articles.title: From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs, and why the connection is complicated
articles.summary: Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find…

image.caption: From rotten food and sexual behavior to political beliefs, researchers want to know how different forms of disgust relate to our attitudesImage: picture alliance

blocks.text: Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.

Psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.
One explanation begins with evolution.
"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.
What are the three types of disgust?
But disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale, developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:

items: Pathogen disgust: Reactions to potential sources of infection, such as rotten food, vomit or bodily waste.
Sexual disgust: Reactions to particular sexual behaviors or situations.
Moral disgust: Reactions to wrongdoing, such as betrayal or cruelty. Researchers debate whether this reflects physical revulsion or moral disapproval.

blocks.text: One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump used language evoking contagion when describing immigrants early in his 2024 presidential campaignImage: Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.
"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.

Indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe."
Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.
"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar said.
Do liberals and conservatives feel disgust differently?
Disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.
A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.

Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.
However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.
Can our bodies reveal our politics?
Some early studies suggested conservatives showed stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.
Many US voters are undecided, disillusioned or disengaged
But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.
Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.
"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.
How do gut feelings influence political beliefs?
Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.

Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.
"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it."
The researchers surveyed 632 US adults, asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility."
They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.
But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.
What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.

blocks.caption: Pathogen disgust is one type of disgust thought to have evolved to protect us from infectionImage: Elena Shishkina/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: "People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.
Can disgust actually be measured?
Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.
He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.
Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.
"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar said.
The new study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.
Inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best."
How might politicians exploit feelings of disgust?
Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.
"I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.
Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.
What's behind the rising polarization in German politics?
"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he said.
Does disgust influence how people vote?

The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.
"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.
Inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he said.
"It's one of the many influences on people's politics."
Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.
He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.
"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said.
